harder.why_harder: Gemology literature emphasizes intrinsic physical properties (hardness, optical qualities, geological rarity) as value determinants, while economics/market-behavior research documents cartel supply controls and manufactured scarcity (e.g., De Beers diamond stockpiling). A survey-strong system can retrieve both framings separately, but reconciling them requires reasoning about the interaction between material properties and market structure: why intrinsic qualities don't determine price independently of supply manipulation, or how physical properties enable but don't guarantee high valuation. The system must recognize that 'rarity' in gemology texts often conflates geological scarcity with market availability.

attempts.answer:
Summary
Gems command high prices because value in gem markets is driven by multiple interacting mechanisms: objectively limited supply and high extraction/processing costs, durable- and durable-goods dynamics, strategic market control that sustains artificial scarcity, strong demand-side signals for status and symbolism, and layered value chains with certification and appraisal that convert attributes into premium prices. Supply restriction is real in places (e.g., via monopoly control, selective distribution, and hoarding) and also artificial (e.g., marketing campaigns and opaque trade practices), but credible scarcity plus perceived desirability yields rents that justify premium prices and robust secondary markets. <cite id="7c0cb106-0">A monopolistic supply historically prevented the diamond market from “breaking down,” and a simple microeconomic model shows a monopoly can sustain slowly but continually rising prices in durable-goods markets</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-3">De Beers maintained global rough-diamond supply via its Central Selling Organization, selling only to handpicked sightholders and stockpiling during oversupply to stabilize prices</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-2">De Beers also actively restricted supply and marketed “artificial scarcity” with the slogan “A Diamond Is Forever,” transforming a common gemstone into a symbol of eternal love and wealth</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-1">Scarcity, quality, origin, and customer attractiveness directly affect price for colored gemstones</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">Colored gemstone value chains are complex and heterogeneous, with many artisanal mines and few large-scale operations, and valuation hinges on assessing scarcity and quality</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-3">High direct costs of exploration, exploitation, and industrial processing are embedded in the final price of finished products</cite><cite id="61b66ea8-1">Auction houses act as key intermediaries that concentrate buyers and sellers, shaping price formation in luxury markets</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-4">Conspicuous prices themselves increase demand by signaling status, producing an upward-sloping effective demand curve for luxury goods like diamonds</cite><cite id="f266030a-0">In virtual economies, supply caps and random drops create artificial scarcity, enabling rapid resale and speculation that inflates secondary-market prices</cite>.

1) Natural scarcity and costliness
Gem-forming geological processes concentrate high-quality crystals suitable for jewelry in limited localizations, and extracting, sorting, cutting, and polishing are capital- and labor-intensive. These constraints create real scarcity at the top end (e.g., large, vivid “A-graded” stones) and high incremental costs per additional unit, which support price premia and discourage over-supply shocks. <cite id="a2fb7fe6-0">Rubies and sapphires concentrate in specific geographies (e.g., Myanmar, Thailand, Madagascar), with some origins (like Kashmir sapphires) commanding the highest prices</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-1">Ruby’s vivid red color, transparency, and hardness drive demand; scarcity and limited supply, along with quality, size, and origin, jointly raise price</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-3">The final price of finished products includes the direct costs of geological exploration and exploitation and of industrial processing and treatment</cite>. Such costliness also underpins durability-based monopoly power: once extracted, a diamond cannot be recreated, so a monopolist can credibly credibly limit supply, raise prices, and deter entry by buyers facing durable-goods problems. <cite id="7c0cb106-0">A monopolistic supply is a necessary condition to prevent the diamond market from breaking down, and the durability of diamonds enables a monopolist to raise and sustain prices over time</cite>.

2) Supply restriction that is real—and that is artificial
Large upstream firms can restrict supply through ownership, contracting, and deliberate pacing. <cite id="7c0cb106-3">De Beers owned or had exclusive contracts with most major mining interests and distributed supplies via periodic sales to carefully selected sightholders, controlling what entered the rough market and stockpiling to keep polished-diamond prices stable</cite>. This vertical integration and selective distribution limit the number of intermediaries who can access supply, sustain scarcity narratives, and capture rents. <cite id="7c0cb106-1">De Beers sold only to handpicked sightholders and relied on downstream merchants’ expertise to route rough to their “most valuable use,” sharing monopoly rents while ensuring value-maximizing cutting and marketing</cite>. Marketing and signaling transform “artificial scarcity” into perceived rarity: <cite id="7c0cb106-2">by restricting supply and advertising “a diamond is forever,” De Beers created artificial scarcity and attached emotional and symbolic value, driving exorbitant prices even though diamonds are not very rare in geological terms</cite>. For colored gems, opaque value chains and selective provenance elevate prices: <cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">valuation hinges on scarcity/quality and origin; reputation and trust-based networks govern trade, with certification initiatives (e.g., Gübelin, Everledger) creating digital provenance to address transparency and authenticity concerns</cite>.

3) Demand-side psychology: status, signaling, and investment narratives
Gems are luxury goods whose demand responds not only to utility but to the price others pay. <cite id="7c0cb106-4">Conspicuous consumption theory shows that higher “conspicuous” prices increase demand by signaling status and others’ impression, producing an upward-sloping effective demand curve for luxury goods; with diamonds, price is both inversely related to quantity via standard demand and positively related to conspicuous price via status signaling</cite>. Advertising and cultural narratives embed gems in rites of passage and social display, turning ownership into a social asset. <cite id="7c0cb106-2">The “Diamonds Are Forever” campaign reframed diamonds as symbols of eternal love, wealth, and power, transforming them from a destructible commodity into an emotional and social asset and multiplying sales from $23 million to $2.1 billion between 1939 and 1979</cite>. This creates a reinforcing loop: as prices rise, demand can rise too because higher prices enhance the status signal, sustaining high prices via demand-side expectations. <cite id="7c0cb106-0">A monopoly can raise and continually increase prices in durable-goods markets, with durability posing the main threat of buyer power via resale/stockpiling</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-4">an upward-sloping effective demand curve emerges when conspicuous price increases the apparent intrinsic preciousness and demand at all price levels</cite>.

4) Price formation, auctions, and appraisals
Auctions and expert intermediaries convert subjective attributes into prices by concentrating demand, benchmarking quality, and managing liquidity. <cite id="61b66ea8-1">Auction houses like Sotheby’s and Christie’s act as key intermediaries in a multi-tier market, concentrating buyers and sellers and shaping price formation for high-end goods</cite><cite id="61b66ea8-3">empirical auction studies show hammer prices adjust to auction design choices like buyer commissions; neutrality of commissions can affect profits without distorting hammer prices</cite>. In practice, scarcity and origin command premiums:
- <cite id="a2fb7fe6-0">Kashmir sapphires command some of the highest prices, and ethical sourcing concerns and undisclosed “doctoring” of lower-quality stones raise quality-assurance costs and shape premiums</cite>.
- <cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">Buyers lack transparency on origin, authenticity, and quality, so they expect provenance and certification to mitigate risk; blockchain-backed provenance (e.g., Everledger) aims to create digital twins and role-specific uploads across the value chain</cite>.
These mechanisms stabilize and elevate prices by linking attributes to verifiable provenance and liquidity events, while opaque middlemen and informal transactions can inflate costs and erode trust. <cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">Transactions are based on mutual trust and reputation with substantial informal trade, creating transparency challenges for financing, insurance, and ethical standards</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-1">price depends on supply and demand, color/quality, size, origin, market trends, and investment needs</cite>.

5) Artificial scarcity in digital/synthetic economies (illustrates the general mechanism)
Massive multiplayer and blockchain games demonstrate the same scarcity-engine logic at scale: fixed supply inventories, rare-drop rates, and hoarding/speculation drive secondary prices. <cite id="f266030a-0">Virtual economies show that developers cap inventories and set low base drop rates for rare gems, enabling rapid accumulation of scarce items and enabling sellers to sell into a waiting liquidity pool; this produces large price swings and speculative demand that inflate secondary-market prices</cite>. The same dynamic appears in real assets when legal scarcity is imposed: <cite id="61b66ea8-2">in the wildlife-gem trade, helmeted hornbill plumes were auctioned thousands of times across Chinese and English platforms, with over 800 lots transacted and average prices $5,065 per item, demonstrating how scarcity and platform intermediation translate into high realized prices</cite>. These cases underscore that whether scarcity is geological or engineered, credible scarcity plus demand yields rents.

6) Why “artificial” restriction still commands high prices
Critics argue some scarcity is manufactured, yet manufactured scarcity can be costly and credible. <cite id="7c0cb106-2">Restricting supply required heavy coordination across mining, refining, distribution, and marketing, with multi-decade campaigns to create psychological scarcity and attach symbolic meaning</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-1">De Beers’ distribution control and selective sightholder relationships were expensive to maintain, but they sustained monopoly rents and prevented supply shocks by directing rough to value-maximizing uses</cite>. Artificial scarcity is reinforced by:
- Opaque valuation: <cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">buyers face high information asymmetry; scarcity/origin and quality assessments by experts translate directly into price</cite>.
- Investment demand: <cite id="a2fb7fe6-1">appreciation potential and market stability expectations add demand, with price changes affecting jewelry demand via substitutions and consumer purchasing decisions</cite>.
- Legal and platform constraints: <cite id="61b66ea8-2">conservation bans and legal protection (e.g., for helmeted hornbills) reduce supply while international auction platforms sustain demand and price discovery</cite>.
In short, artificial scarcity is “artificial,” but it is embedded in costly, institution-backed value chains and powerful social signals; it is not free creation ex nihilo but strategic management of perceived and real constraints. <cite id="a2fb7fe6-3">Final prices embed real costs of exploration and processing</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-0">durability and monopoly pacing sustain price levels</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-4">conspicuous price increases demand, reinforcing scarcity rents</cite>.

7) Limits and conflicts
Artificial scarcity faces pushback when supply constraints loosen or when transparency collapses. <cite id="7c0cb106-3">New sources resisted De Beers’ control, selling outside the CSO, and the company pivoted to be a buyer of last resort to stabilize prices</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-1">sightholders’ margins shrank as De Beers adjusted distribution and pricing, provoking rivalry</cite>. Quality fraud and opaque supply chains erode trust and can depress prices. <cite id="a2fb7fe6-0">Undisclosed “doctoring” of lower-quality gemstones undermines authentication and ethical sourcing, prompting premium premiums for trusted provenance</cite>. Legal protections can reduce supply and raise prices, but also invite alternative markets and enforcement costs. <cite id="61b66ea8-2">Helmeted hornbill parts saw rising auction volumes and prices historically, and legal protections shifted trading to online platforms while sustaining demand</cite>.

Bottom line
Gems command high prices because scarcity—real or artificial—meets durable, costly-to-produce assets whose value is amplified by status signaling and expert-certified provenance. Monopolistic and cartel-like supply control, selective distribution, and advertising create credible scarcity constraints and elevate demand via conspicuous prices, while auctions and certification convert attributes into liquid price premiums. <cite id="7c0cb106-0">Monopoly control plus durability yields slowly rising prices</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-2">artificial scarcity and branding transform perception into value</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-3">stockpiling and selective sales stabilize and lift prices</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-1">scarcity, origin, and quality move colored gem prices</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">trust-based value chains and provenance certification underpin premiums</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-4">conspicuous price raises demand, supporting scarcity rents</cite><cite id="f266030a-0">engineered supply caps in virtual economies inflate secondary prices via scarce drops and speculation</cite>.

These are followed by traders that have either a regional, national, or international customer networks, refiners with diverse specializations in terms of cut and treatment, exporters, regional, national, and international wholesalers, jewelers, and retail brands [18]. Utilisation of local gemstones reflects their appropriate physical characteristics and corresponding mineralogical qualities (Balakirev et al., 1979). Their prospective profitability for the industry depends on the value of raw materials and the current market price of jewellery products (Smith, 1980;Rid, 1986;Kornilov & Solodova, 1986). Coloured stones from central Asia have long been preferred for their appealing appearance (e.g., Goodwin, 1996;Pugachenkova, 1996;Domínguez-Bella, 2018). The most expensive jewellery decorations and luxury goods have been made from rare, mainly transparent, gemstones. Local quality and quantity of diamonds do not allow for their use in the jewel trade. For this purpose, particularly bright and more widely distributed, high-quality minerals such as coloured tourmalines and rock crystals are employed. An even higher potential for Kazakhstan, as well as the Russian Gorno Altay gemstone industry, can be ascribed to decorative and easy-to-work semi-precious stones with rich regional resources, such as jasper, agate and chalcedony (Fig. 10A, B). Of certain importance are deposits of decorative rocks used for building constructions and home interior industry purposes, such as coloured granites, gneiss or marbles (Fig. 9C-F), the resources of which are fairly opulent in the country (Beldeeva & Somin, 2014). The most valuable precious stones of Kazakhstan (sapphire, ruby, topaz, chrysoprase and turquoise) are often combined with precious metals (gold, platinum and silver). The final price of the finished products reflects, except for the raw gemstone value, the direct costs of geological exploration and exploitation and of industrial processing/ treatment of those materials. Among the semi-precious stones, the bulk-carved minerals such as jasper or fine-grained coloured quartz are mainly used for artwork and souvenirs. The widely distributed hard rocks with suitable mechanical qualities, such granites or marbles, are used as decorative materials.

Snippet: Fine art auction houses are famously resilient organisations. Sotheby's and Christie's, the two largest auction houses in the world, have existed since 1744 and 1766 respectively, accounting in 2016 for almost half of the $16.9 billion global auction market ( Fig. 2; Heath Pownall, 2017). The rise of British art auctioneers, such as Christie's, Sotheby's, Phillips and Bonhams, is largely attributed to the excessive supply of fine art consigned to Britain by the displaced French aristocracy during the aftermath of the French Revolution in 1789 (Bellingham, 2016). For centuries, the British aristocracy has built strong connections with the two main auction houses, Sotheby's and Christie's, forming a loyal clientele with an appetite for cultural consumption. However, the role of auction houses changed at the beginning of the 20th century to mainly supplying the 'wholesale' secondary market and selling to art dealers.

Auction houses constitute an important intermediary within the art market, concentrating buyers and sellers in a single location. The auction industry is generally considered to be a three-tier market (Caves, 2000), and each of the three tiers encounters different conditions of risk and uncertainty. The first tier of high-end auction houses, based on the volume of art trade, consists of auction houses such as Christie's and Sotheby's (Pownall, 2017). These auction houses face uncertainty when sourcing valuable artworks, as fierce competition reduces their bargaining power over consigners, leading them to take significant risks, including the provision of financial guarantees to secure consignments (Adam, 2014;Heath, 2012). The second tier resembles the first by trading in "highly-valuable and well-known" collectibles worldwide, although in lower volume (Caves, 2000: 334). Second-tier auction houses are mainly concerned with staging a limited number of highquality, often niche-market auctions, such as in design (e.g. Phillips) or antiques (e.g. Bonhams); for them, shifting trends like the rise of contemporary art can become an important source of uncertainty. Summary
Gems command high prices because value in gem markets is driven by multiple interacting mechanisms: objectively limited supply and high extraction/processing costs, durable- and durable-goods dynamics, strategic market control that sustains artificial scarcity, strong demand-side signals for status and symbolism, and layered value chains with certification and appraisal that convert attributes into premium prices. Supply restriction is real in places (e.g., via monopoly control, selective distribution, and hoarding) and also artificial (e.g., marketing campaigns and opaque trade practices), but credible scarcity plus perceived desirability yields rents that justify premium prices and robust secondary markets. <cite id="7c0cb106-0">A monopolistic supply historically prevented the diamond market from “breaking down,” and a simple microeconomic model shows a monopoly can sustain slowly but continually rising prices in durable-goods markets</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-3">De Beers maintained global rough-diamond supply via its Central Selling Organization, selling only to handpicked sightholders and stockpiling during oversupply to stabilize prices</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-2">De Beers also actively restricted supply and marketed “artificial scarcity” with the slogan “A Diamond Is Forever,” transforming a common gemstone into a symbol of eternal love and wealth</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-1">Scarcity, quality, origin, and customer attractiveness directly affect price for colored gemstones</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">Colored gemstone value chains are complex and heterogeneous, with many artisanal mines and few large-scale operations, and valuation hinges on assessing scarcity and quality</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-3">High direct costs of exploration, exploitation, and industrial processing are embedded in the final price of finished products</cite><cite id="61b66ea8-1">Auction houses act as key intermediaries that concentrate buyers and sellers, shaping price formation in luxury markets</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-4">Conspicuous prices themselves increase demand by signaling status, producing an upward-sloping effective demand curve for luxury goods like diamonds</cite><cite id="f266030a-0">In virtual economies, supply caps and random drops create artificial scarcity, enabling rapid resale and speculation that inflates secondary-market prices</cite>.

1) Natural scarcity and costliness
Gem-forming geological processes concentrate high-quality crystals suitable for jewelry in limited localizations, and extracting, sorting, cutting, and polishing are capital- and labor-intensive. These constraints create real scarcity at the top end (e.g., large, vivid “A-graded” stones) and high incremental costs per additional unit, which support price premia and discourage over-supply shocks. <cite id="a2fb7fe6-0">Rubies and sapphires concentrate in specific geographies (e.g., Myanmar, Thailand, Madagascar), with some origins (like Kashmir sapphires) commanding the highest prices</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-1">Ruby’s vivid red color, transparency, and hardness drive demand; scarcity and limited supply, along with quality, size, and origin, jointly raise price</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-3">The final price of finished products includes the direct costs of geological exploration and exploitation and of industrial processing and treatment</cite>. Such costliness also underpins durability-based monopoly power: once extracted, a diamond cannot be recreated, so a monopolist can credibly credibly limit supply, raise prices, and deter entry by buyers facing durable-goods problems. <cite id="7c0cb106-0">A monopolistic supply is a necessary condition to prevent the diamond market from breaking down, and the durability of diamonds enables a monopolist to raise and sustain prices over time</cite>.

2) Supply restriction that is real—and that is artificial
Large upstream firms can restrict supply through ownership, contracting, and deliberate pacing. <cite id="7c0cb106-3">De Beers owned or had exclusive contracts with most major mining interests and distributed supplies via periodic sales to carefully selected sightholders, controlling what entered the rough market and stockpiling to keep polished-diamond prices stable</cite>. This vertical integration and selective distribution limit the number of intermediaries who can access supply, sustain scarcity narratives, and capture rents. <cite id="7c0cb106-1">De Beers sold only to handpicked sightholders and relied on downstream merchants’ expertise to route rough to their “most valuable use,” sharing monopoly rents while ensuring value-maximizing cutting and marketing</cite>. Marketing and signaling transform “artificial scarcity” into perceived rarity: <cite id="7c0cb106-2">by restricting supply and advertising “a diamond is forever,” De Beers created artificial scarcity and attached emotional and symbolic value, driving exorbitant prices even though diamonds are not very rare in geological terms</cite>. For colored gems, opaque value chains and selective provenance elevate prices: <cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">valuation hinges on scarcity/quality and origin; reputation and trust-based networks govern trade, with certification initiatives (e.g., Gübelin, Everledger) creating digital provenance to address transparency and authenticity concerns</cite>.

3) Demand-side psychology: status, signaling, and investment narratives
Gems are luxury goods whose demand responds not only to utility but to the price others pay. <cite id="7c0cb106-4">Conspicuous consumption theory shows that higher “conspicuous” prices increase demand by signaling status and others’ impression, producing an upward-sloping effective demand curve for luxury goods; with diamonds, price is both inversely related to quantity via standard demand and positively related to conspicuous price via status signaling</cite>. Advertising and cultural narratives embed gems in rites of passage and social display, turning ownership into a social asset. <cite id="7c0cb106-2">The “Diamonds Are Forever” campaign reframed diamonds as symbols of eternal love, wealth, and power, transforming them from a destructible commodity into an emotional and social asset and multiplying sales from $23 million to $2.1 billion between 1939 and 1979</cite>. This creates a reinforcing loop: as prices rise, demand can rise too because higher prices enhance the status signal, sustaining high prices via demand-side expectations. <cite id="7c0cb106-0">A monopoly can raise and continually increase prices in durable-goods markets, with durability posing the main threat of buyer power via resale/stockpiling</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-4">an upward-sloping effective demand curve emerges when conspicuous price increases the apparent intrinsic preciousness and demand at all price levels</cite>.

4) Price formation, auctions, and appraisals
Auctions and expert intermediaries convert subjective attributes into prices by concentrating demand, benchmarking quality, and managing liquidity. <cite id="61b66ea8-1">Auction houses like Sotheby’s and Christie’s act as key intermediaries in a multi-tier market, concentrating buyers and sellers and shaping price formation for high-end goods</cite><cite id="61b66ea8-3">empirical auction studies show hammer prices adjust to auction design choices like buyer commissions; neutrality of commissions can affect profits without distorting hammer prices</cite>. In practice, scarcity and origin command premiums:
- <cite id="a2fb7fe6-0">Kashmir sapphires command some of the highest prices, and ethical sourcing concerns and undisclosed “doctoring” of lower-quality stones raise quality-assurance costs and shape premiums</cite>.
- <cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">Buyers lack transparency on origin, authenticity, and quality, so they expect provenance and certification to mitigate risk; blockchain-backed provenance (e.g., Everledger) aims to create digital twins and role-specific uploads across the value chain</cite>.
These mechanisms stabilize and elevate prices by linking attributes to verifiable provenance and liquidity events, while opaque middlemen and informal transactions can inflate costs and erode trust. <cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">Transactions are based on mutual trust and reputation with substantial informal trade, creating transparency challenges for financing, insurance, and ethical standards</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-1">price depends on supply and demand, color/quality, size, origin, market trends, and investment needs</cite>.

5) Artificial scarcity in digital/synthetic economies (illustrates the general mechanism)
Massive multiplayer and blockchain games demonstrate the same scarcity-engine logic at scale: fixed supply inventories, rare-drop rates, and hoarding/speculation drive secondary prices. <cite id="f266030a-0">Virtual economies show that developers cap inventories and set low base drop rates for rare gems, enabling rapid accumulation of scarce items and enabling sellers to sell into a waiting liquidity pool; this produces large price swings and speculative demand that inflate secondary-market prices</cite>. The same dynamic appears in real assets when legal scarcity is imposed: <cite id="61b66ea8-2">in the wildlife-gem trade, helmeted hornbill plumes were auctioned thousands of times across Chinese and English platforms, with over 800 lots transacted and average prices $5,065 per item, demonstrating how scarcity and platform intermediation translate into high realized prices</cite>. These cases underscore that whether scarcity is geological or engineered, credible scarcity plus demand yields rents.

6) Why “artificial” restriction still commands high prices
Critics argue some scarcity is manufactured, yet manufactured scarcity can be costly and credible. <cite id="7c0cb106-2">Restricting supply required heavy coordination across mining, refining, distribution, and marketing, with multi-decade campaigns to create psychological scarcity and attach symbolic meaning</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-1">De Beers’ distribution control and selective sightholder relationships were expensive to maintain, but they sustained monopoly rents and prevented supply shocks by directing rough to value-maximizing uses</cite>. Artificial scarcity is reinforced by:
- Opaque valuation: <cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">buyers face high information asymmetry; scarcity/origin and quality assessments by experts translate directly into price</cite>.
- Investment demand: <cite id="a2fb7fe6-1">appreciation potential and market stability expectations add demand, with price changes affecting jewelry demand via substitutions and consumer purchasing decisions</cite>.
- Legal and platform constraints: <cite id="61b66ea8-2">conservation bans and legal protection (e.g., for helmeted hornbills) reduce supply while international auction platforms sustain demand and price discovery</cite>.
In short, artificial scarcity is “artificial,” but it is embedded in costly, institution-backed value chains and powerful social signals; it is not free creation ex nihilo but strategic management of perceived and real constraints. <cite id="a2fb7fe6-3">Final prices embed real costs of exploration and processing</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-0">durability and monopoly pacing sustain price levels</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-4">conspicuous price increases demand, reinforcing scarcity rents</cite>.

7) Limits and conflicts
Artificial scarcity faces pushback when supply constraints loosen or when transparency collapses. <cite id="7c0cb106-3">New sources resisted De Beers’ control, selling outside the CSO, and the company pivoted to be a buyer of last resort to stabilize prices</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-1">sightholders’ margins shrank as De Beers adjusted distribution and pricing, provoking rivalry</cite>. Quality fraud and opaque supply chains erode trust and can depress prices. <cite id="a2fb7fe6-0">Undisclosed “doctoring” of lower-quality gemstones undermines authentication and ethical sourcing, prompting premium premiums for trusted provenance</cite>. Legal protections can reduce supply and raise prices, but also invite alternative markets and enforcement costs. <cite id="61b66ea8-2">Helmeted hornbill parts saw rising auction volumes and prices historically, and legal protections shifted trading to online platforms while sustaining demand</cite>.

Bottom line
Gems command high prices because scarcity—real or artificial—meets durable, costly-to-produce assets whose value is amplified by status signaling and expert-certified provenance. Monopolistic and cartel-like supply control, selective distribution, and advertising create credible scarcity constraints and elevate demand via conspicuous prices, while auctions and certification convert attributes into liquid price premiums. <cite id="7c0cb106-0">Monopoly control plus durability yields slowly rising prices</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-2">artificial scarcity and branding transform perception into value</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-3">stockpiling and selective sales stabilize and lift prices</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-1">scarcity, origin, and quality move colored gem prices</cite><cite id="a2fb7fe6-2">trust-based value chains and provenance certification underpin premiums</cite><cite id="7c0cb106-4">conspicuous price raises demand, supporting scarcity rents</cite><cite id="f266030a-0">engineered supply caps in virtual economies inflate secondary prices via scarce drops and speculation</cite>.</answer>

Title: A Simple Microeconomic Model Illustrating Rising Diamond Prices and the Durable Goods Problem
Snippet: A Simple Microeconomic Model Illustrating Rising Diamond Prices and the Durable Goods Problem The worldwide market for gemstone diamonds is full of anomalies and peculiarities. Gemstone diamonds are often purchased because they are expensive. After the end of the 19th century the diamond market was controlled by a worldwide monopoly, and later by a cartel which in turn was firmly controlled by the former monopolist - De Beers. The existence of a monopolistic supply is a necessary condition to prevent the diamond market from breaking down. Using a simple microeconomic model the paper investigates how the monopoly creates prices which increase slowly but continually. In addition, we discuss problems threatening the monopoly. However, the major problem is the durability of the diamond. This may cause the diamond monopoly to be threatened by an uncontrollable competitor - previous purchasers, as stated theoretically in the Coase conjecture.

In fact, De Beers' vertically integrated strategies help explain some curiosities of the prior strategy. Economic theory implies that an upstream monopolist maximizes profit when downstream markets are competitive. Yet De Beers, in contrast to theory, sold only to handpicked dealers. Moreover, and similarly in contrast to theory, diamond merchants have clamored to become a sightholder atop the distribution stream, which suggests that De Beers sells diamonds to sightholders at less than the monopoly price and instead shares with them some monopoly rents. The reason for De Beers' curious distribution strategy is that it relied on these merchants to ensure that rough stones were directed to their most valuable use. It therefore selected as sightholders merchants who were deeply familiar with the diamond trade to know how to cut, distribute, and market diamonds to create maximum value. In short, De Beers relied on downstream merchants' market information and industry expertise, and the company implemented a pricing strategy that economically sustained these knowledgeable intermediaries.

The industry's longtime intermediaries-especially mid-size and small operators who do not partner with leading retail chains-are both the primary victims of this new pricing strategy and the most vulnerable. Compared with the upstream production and downstream retail markets, this intermediate market for distributing and cutting rough diamonds has long offered the slimmest margins (see Figure 5), and producers' pricing efforts have caused these margins to continue to shrink. Consequently, De Beers' new strategy has had major reverberations throughout the diamond distribution chain.

Whenever supply began to exceed demand and threatened to dampen market prices for polished diamonds, the company would show its determination to be a buyer of last resort, stockpiling rough gems to sustain stable prices (Spar 2000, 5, 9-10).

snippet.text: A Simple Microeconomic Model Illustrating Rising Diamond Prices and the Durable Goods Problem The worldwide market for gemstone diamonds is full of anomalies and peculiarities. Gemstone diamonds are often purchased because they are expensive. After the end of the 19th century the diamond market was controlled by a worldwide monopoly, and later by a cartel which in turn was firmly controlled by the former monopolist - De Beers. The existence of a monopolistic supply is a necessary condition to prevent the diamond market from breaking down. Using a simple microeconomic model the paper investigates how the monopoly creates prices which increase slowly but continually. In addition, we discuss problems threatening the monopoly. However, the major problem is the durability of the diamond. This may cause the diamond monopoly to be threatened by an uncontrollable competitor - previous purchasers, as stated theoretically in the Coase conjecture.

In fact, De Beers' vertically integrated strategies help explain some curiosities of the prior strategy. Economic theory implies that an upstream monopolist maximizes profit when downstream markets are competitive. Yet De Beers, in contrast to theory, sold only to handpicked dealers. Moreover, and similarly in contrast to theory, diamond merchants have clamored to become a sightholder atop the distribution stream, which suggests that De Beers sells diamonds to sightholders at less than the monopoly price and instead shares with them some monopoly rents. The reason for De Beers' curious distribution strategy is that it relied on these merchants to ensure that rough stones were directed to their most valuable use. It therefore selected as sightholders merchants who were deeply familiar with the diamond trade to know how to cut, distribute, and market diamonds to create maximum value. In short, De Beers relied on downstream merchants' market information and industry expertise, and the company implemented a pricing strategy that economically sustained these knowledgeable intermediaries.

The industry's longtime intermediaries-especially mid-size and small operators who do not partner with leading retail chains-are both the primary victims of this new pricing strategy and the most vulnerable. Compared with the upstream production and downstream retail markets, this intermediate market for distributing and cutting rough diamonds has long offered the slimmest margins (see Figure 5), and producers' pricing efforts have caused these margins to continue to shrink. Consequently, De Beers' new strategy has had major reverberations throughout the diamond distribution chain.

The story of the success of De Beers' creative idea is a testimony of the fact that successful advertising needs a subtle understanding of human psychology. Since the discovery of a large number of South African diamond mines in 1870, the supply of diamonds was in abundance. When De Beers was established in 1888, it started stockpiling diamonds to manipulate prices -by means of controlling all areas from mining, refining, distribution & even to marketing, with a view to establish themselves as the price setters! De Beers had to find out a method to control the demand and supply of this gemstone in the world. By restricting supply, the diamonds were created as rare gemstones. And therefore, unique and special. In fact, it created a strong feeling of artificial scarcity -which even now gets reflected in the exorbitant prices of diamonds. In reality, diamonds are not very rare but are one of the more common gemstones! An advertising agency was then hired in 1938 and a narrative was created around the product. It started a campaign, and the impact was tremendous. Even though diamonds are destructible and technically would not last "forever" -De Beers started creating an emotional appeal by selling their diamonds with the slogan "a diamond is forever", making diamonds a symbol of eternal love. The sales of the company started skyrocketing from $23 million to $ 2.1 billion between 1939 and 1979. And before anyone could realize the diamonds became not only a pricy possession but also an emotional asset -a symbol of true love and long-lasting commitment! The gemstone has now become a new symbol of wealth, power, and ultimate love. 

Thus, the credit goes to De Beers for establishing this successful industry through a novel marketing approach. "A Diamond Is Forever" these four words became iconic and have appeared in all De Beers advertisements since then. They revolutionized the way people perceive diamonds -compelling them to buy for their loved ones and thus changing scenario for the entire diamond industry as a whole. De Beers devised a new marketing strategy, instead of marketing the product, they marketed the value.

Writing about De Beers' approach to the year 2000, a Harvard Business School case study observed:

De Beers was accustomed to chaos. The company thrived on it, and had long ago learned to master it. But the millennium posed new challenges-serious challenges with the potential to undermine De Beers's legendary power and compel a rethinking of its strategy (Spar 2000, p. 2).

The accustomed "chaos" is the vicissitudes of a volatile commodities market combined with the demand elasticity of luxury goods, and De Beers' success rested on its ability to assert control throughout diamond market. For nearly a century, De Beers enjoyed monopoly control over the sale and distribution of rough diamonds. It either owned or secured exclusive contracts with a majority of the world's mining interests, and through its central selling organization (CSO) it distributed its supplies deliberately through "sightholders," a collection of approximately 125 carefully selected distributors chosen to receive and purchase caches of De Beers rough diamonds ten times each year. Sitting atop the diamond distribution chain, De Beers was able to control global supply of rough diamonds by carefully controlling what was sold each year, and it invested in sustaining global demand through creative advertising strategies and directing distribution chains. Whenever additional sources of rough diamonds threatened to enter the market, De Beers swiftly entered into exclusive purchasing arrangements with the new suppliers (Spar 2000, p. 5). Whenever supply began to exceed demand and threatened to dampen market prices for polished diamonds, the company would show its determination to be a buyer of last resort, stockpiling rough gems to sustain stable prices (Spar 2000, 5, 9-10).

In the late 1990s, however, this decades-old strategy started to fray, and changes to diamond supply "began to hint at a very different structure for the world's diamond market and . . . De Beers" (Spar 2000, p. 9). Diamond mines discovered in Australia in the 1980s and in Canada in the 1990s began resisting De Beers' control and started selling rough diamonds outside De Beers' CSO in 1996; De Beers' agreement to purchase Russia's enormous production, formed in 1990 during Russia's desperate need for hard currency, expired in 1995, and, after a year of Russian diamonds "leaking" into the global market, the Russian company Alrosa began distributing

Title: Beyond Task-technology Fit: Exploring Network Value of Blockchain Technology Based on Two Supply Chain Cases
Snippet: Industry: The colored gemstone industry reveals three peculiarities. First, the stones vary largely in their value per carat, depending on the characteristics of the stone, such as scarcity, quality, origin, and customer attractiveness. Hence, assessing the characteristics of a stone is key for evaluating the value of a colored gemstone. Second, the value chain in the colored gemstone industry is highly complex and heterogeneous. There are many artisanal mines and only a few large-scale mines with heavy machinery on the mining stage. These are followed by traders that have either a regional, national, or international customer networks, refiners with diverse specializations in terms of cut and treatment, exporters, regional, national, and international wholesalers, jewelers, and retail brands [18]. Third, the transactions within the industry are based on mutual trust and reputation between transaction partners (e.g., miners and regional traders). A large volume of the trade is informal with limited transparency for external parties, causing substantial challenges for financing, insurance, and ethical standards. The previously described three peculiarities turned into a burden given the lack of transparency in the industry. First, for end-customers or upstream actors (e.g., retail brands), the actions of previous stages in the value chain are not transparent given the complexity and heterogeneity of the value chain as well as the informal transactions. Hence, buyers fear to finance unethical or ecological harmful actions in the downstream value chain. Second, end-customer as layperson having a hard time assessing the characteristics of a stone and its value. Consequently, end-customers are expecting more transparency on aspects such as origin, authenticity, and physical qualities. 

Blockchain application: Against this backdrop, Gübelin Gem Lab1 and Everledger2 introduced the Provenance Proof Blockchain3 for the colored gemstone industry. The blockchain solutions allow creating a digital twin for each colored gemstone and storing all relevant information (e.g., physical dimensions, color, cut) along the value chain. Each stage in the value chain has its own role and enables to upload of role-specific information.

Title: Gemstones of eastern Kazakhstan
Snippet: As presented above, the territory of eastern Kazakhstan with its complex structural formations, hosts a diversity of gemstones suitable for both jewel and artwork processing. Utilisation of local gemstones reflects their appropriate physical characteristics and corresponding mineralogical qualities (Balakirev et al., 1979). Their prospective profitability for the industry depends on the value of raw materials and the current market price of jewellery products (Smith, 1980;Rid, 1986;Kornilov & Solodova, 1986). Coloured stones from central Asia have long been preferred for their appealing appearance (e.g., Goodwin, 1996;Pugachenkova, 1996;Domínguez-Bella, 2018). The most expensive jewellery decorations and luxury goods have been made from rare, mainly transparent, gemstones. Local quality and quantity of diamonds do not allow for their use in the jewel trade. For this purpose, particularly bright and more widely distributed, high-quality minerals such as coloured tourmalines and rock crystals are employed. An even higher potential for Kazakhstan, as well as the Russian Gorno Altay gemstone industry, can be ascribed to decorative and easy-to-work semi-precious stones with rich regional resources, such as jasper, agate and chalcedony (Fig. 10A, B). Of certain importance are deposits of decorative rocks used for building constructions and home interior industry purposes, such as coloured granites, gneiss or marbles (Fig. 9C-F), the resources of which are fairly opulent in the country (Beldeeva & Somin, 2014). The most valuable precious stones of Kazakhstan (sapphire, ruby, topaz, chrysoprase and turquoise) are often combined with precious metals (gold, platinum and silver). The final price of the finished products reflects, except for the raw gemstone value, the direct costs of geological exploration and exploitation and of industrial processing/ treatment of those materials. Among the semi-precious stones, the bulk-carved minerals such as jasper or fine-grained coloured quartz are mainly used for artwork and souvenirs. The widely distributed hard rocks with suitable mechanical qualities, such granites or marbles, are used as decorative materials.

Application of gemstones has changed significantly during the last decades in connection with the development of exact instruments in high-tech industrial and laboratory employments

Movements in ruby prices may also be affected by external factors.

Factors such as supply and demand, market stability, changes in consumer demand and external factors interact to determine the price trend in the ruby market. Participants in the jewelry industry should pay close attention to changes in ruby prices and make appropriate adjustments and decisions based on market conditions.

Industry: The colored gemstone industry reveals three peculiarities. First, the stones vary largely in their value per carat, depending on the characteristics of the stone, such as scarcity, quality, origin, and customer attractiveness. Hence, assessing the characteristics of a stone is key for evaluating the value of a colored gemstone. Second, the value chain in the colored gemstone industry is highly complex and heterogeneous. There are many artisanal mines and only a few large-scale mines with heavy machinery on the mining stage. These are followed by traders that have either a regional, national, or international customer networks, refiners with diverse specializations in terms of cut and treatment, exporters, regional, national, and international wholesalers, jewelers, and retail brands [18]. Third, the transactions within the industry are based on mutual trust and reputation between transaction partners (e.g., miners and regional traders). A large volume of the trade is informal with limited transparency for external parties, causing substantial challenges for financing, insurance, and ethical standards. The previously described three peculiarities turned into a burden given the lack of transparency in the industry. First, for end-customers or upstream actors (e.g., retail brands), the actions of previous stages in the value chain are not transparent given the complexity and heterogeneity of the value chain as well as the informal transactions. Hence, buyers fear to finance unethical or ecological harmful actions in the downstream value chain. Second, end-customer as layperson having a hard time assessing the characteristics of a stone and its value. Consequently, end-customers are expecting more transparency on aspects such as origin, authenticity, and physical qualities. 

Blockchain application: Against this backdrop, Gübelin Gem Lab1 and Everledger2 introduced the Provenance Proof Blockchain3 for the colored gemstone industry. The blockchain solutions allow creating a digital twin for each colored gemstone and storing all relevant information (e.g., physical dimensions, color, cut) along the value chain. Each stage in the value chain has its own role and enables to upload of role-specific information.

As presented above, the territory of eastern Kazakhstan with its complex structural formations, hosts a diversity of gemstones suitable for both jewel and artwork processing. Utilisation of local gemstones reflects their appropriate physical characteristics and corresponding mineralogical qualities (Balakirev et al., 1979). Their prospective profitability for the industry depends on the value of raw materials and the current market price of jewellery products (Smith, 1980;Rid, 1986;Kornilov & Solodova, 1986). Coloured stones from central Asia have long been preferred for their appealing appearance (e.g., Goodwin, 1996;Pugachenkova, 1996;Domínguez-Bella, 2018). The most expensive jewellery decorations and luxury goods have been made from rare, mainly transparent, gemstones. Local quality and quantity of diamonds do not allow for their use in the jewel trade. For this purpose, particularly bright and more widely distributed, high-quality minerals such as coloured tourmalines and rock crystals are employed. An even higher potential for Kazakhstan, as well as the Russian Gorno Altay gemstone industry, can be ascribed to decorative and easy-to-work semi-precious stones with rich regional resources, such as jasper, agate and chalcedony (Fig. 10A, B). Of certain importance are deposits of decorative rocks used for building constructions and home interior industry purposes, such as coloured granites, gneiss or marbles (Fig. 9C-F), the resources of which are fairly opulent in the country (Beldeeva & Somin, 2014). The most valuable precious stones of Kazakhstan (sapphire, ruby, topaz, chrysoprase and turquoise) are often combined with precious metals (gold, platinum and silver). The final price of the finished products reflects, except for the raw gemstone value, the direct costs of geological exploration and exploitation and of industrial processing/ treatment of those materials. Among the semi-precious stones, the bulk-carved minerals such as jasper or fine-grained coloured quartz are mainly used for artwork and souvenirs. The widely distributed hard rocks with suitable mechanical qualities, such granites or marbles, are used as decorative materials.

Application of gemstones has changed significantly during the last decades in connection with the development of exact instruments in high-tech industrial and laboratory employments

Ruby is one of the important gemstones in jewelry, and its price changes have an important impact on the entire jewelry market. The supply and demand relationship of ruby is a key factor affecting its price. If supply decreases or demand increases, the price of rubies may increase. Conversely, if supply increases or demand decreases, ruby prices may fall. The stability of ruby prices is crucial to the development of the jewelry market. Large price fluctuations may lead to increased market uncertainty, affecting consumer purchasing decisions and industry stability. Changes in ruby prices may affect consumer demand for ruby jewelry. If prices rise, consumers may look for substitutes or reduce purchases, affecting market demand. On the contrary, lower prices may stimulate consumer interest in purchasing ruby jewelry. Movements in ruby prices may also be affected by external factors. 

Changes in ruby prices have an important impact on the jewelry market. Factors such as supply and demand, market stability, changes in consumer demand and external factors interact to determine the price trend in the ruby market. Participants in the jewelry industry should pay close attention to changes in ruby prices and make appropriate adjustments and decisions based on market conditions.

Title: Uncertainty, strategic sensemaking and organisational failure in the art market: What went wrong with LVMH's investment in Phillips auctioneers?
Snippet: Fine art auction houses are famously resilient organisations. Sotheby's and Christie's, the two largest auction houses in the world, have existed since 1744 and 1766 respectively, accounting in 2016 for almost half of the $16.9 billion global auction market ( Fig. 2; Heath Pownall, 2017). The rise of British art auctioneers, such as Christie's, Sotheby's, Phillips and Bonhams, is largely attributed to the excessive supply of fine art consigned to Britain by the displaced French aristocracy during the aftermath of the French Revolution in 1789 (Bellingham, 2016). For centuries, the British aristocracy has built strong connections with the two main auction houses, Sotheby's and Christie's, forming a loyal clientele with an appetite for cultural consumption. However, the role of auction houses changed at the beginning of the 20th century to mainly supplying the 'wholesale' secondary market and selling to art dealers.

Auction houses constitute an important intermediary within the art market, concentrating buyers and sellers in a single location. The auction industry is generally considered to be a three-tier market (Caves, 2000), and each of the three tiers encounters different conditions of risk and uncertainty. The first tier of high-end auction houses, based on the volume of art trade, consists of auction houses such as Christie's and Sotheby's (Pownall, 2017). These auction houses face uncertainty when sourcing valuable artworks, as fierce competition reduces their bargaining power over consigners, leading them to take significant risks, including the provision of financial guarantees to secure consignments (Adam, 2014;Heath, 2012). The second tier resembles the first by trading in "highly-valuable and well-known" collectibles worldwide, although in lower volume (Caves, 2000: 334). Second-tier auction houses are mainly concerned with staging a limited number of highquality, often niche-market auctions, such as in design (e.g. Phillips) or antiques (e.g. Bonhams); for them, shifting trends like the rise of contemporary art can become an important source of uncertainty. Ashenfelter (1989) specifically examines a 'natural experiment' conducted with wine auctions in London. In the spring of 1986, Sotheby's charged a 10%

Ashenfelter empirically showed that the difference of hammer prices in the spring had vanished in the autumn. Similarly, Marks (2009) uses data from wine auctions in Chicago to demonstrate that hammer prices reflect the buyer's premium. Moreover, Ashenfelter and Graddy (2005, pp. 6, 11) explicitly address that "the entire increase in the buyer's premiums should fall on the seller" and thus buyers "are unlikely to have suffered any injury from the collusion [between Sotheby's and Christie's]." 8

Snippet: To provide an overview of the international auction market of HHPs, we conducted a search of online auction markets across Chinese and English language websites. We searched for all HHP data available on these databases from 1992 to 2020. For auctions in Chinese, we collected data from Artron (artron.net), an art data company and e-platform auction service that assembles data from auction houses across China and contains nearly 4.7 million auction records of Chinese artwork (Chou, 2018). For auctions in English, we collected data from a US-based international auction e-platform, LiveAuctioneers (liveauctioneers.com), which, like Artron, provides an auction service for many auction houses. We also collected data from independent auctioneers Sotheby's (sothebys.com) and Christie's (christies.com) in English. All websites offered online bidding, and data were collected after auctions finished. Both Artron and LiveAuctioneers showcase products from different international auction houses, including Sotheby's and Christie's. In this case, we reported lots only from Sotheby's and Christie's websites, not from Artron or LiveAuctioneers, to avoid duplication of records. Because it was not possible to achieve complete coverage of all auction markets for HHPs, we did not attempt to estimate the size of the market. However, these auction sites are well-known, international, art trade platforms, so we considered it reasonable to assume that the trends and market characteristics we identified would broadly apply to the wider market of which our data represented a sample.

Because it was not possible to achieve complete coverage of all auction markets for HHPs, we did not attempt to estimate the size of the market. attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of why artificial supply restrictions have historically stabilized prices and allocation in the diamond market but have not produced the same systemic effects in colored gemstone markets. The explanation emphasizes market structure, certification and enforcement, supply-side substitutability, and smuggling/gray-market dynamics, with concrete examples and mechanisms.

Summary of the contrast
Artificial supply restriction has “worked” in diamonds because a few vertically integrated producers controlled early supply, coupled with a credible Kimberley Process-style certification and trade chokepoints that let a cartel-like oligopoly enforce scarcity and deter smuggling, keeping rough prices stable even as the formal monopoly eroded <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">De Beers historically dominated diamond sales and used selective selling and stockpiling to create artificial scarcity and manipulate prices</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">With stocked diamonds, De Beers was able to create an artificial scarcity that allowed it to manipulate the price of diamonds around the world</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-2">Despite De Beers’ market share decline to roughly a third by value, average rough/polished prices per carat have increased and producer margins remained high, indicating retained monopolistic features</cite>. By contrast, colored gemstones are produced by many artisanal and small-scale miners in numerous geographies with heterogeneous qualities and low-cost processing hubs, fragmented certification, and high smuggling and rebranding fraud, undermining any centralized scarcity regime <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">The colored gemstone value chain is highly complex and heterogeneous, with many artisanal mines and informal transactions that limit transparency</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-3">Sapphires from Africa are often smuggled to Sri Lanka and sold as “Ceylon sapphires,” with about 70% of Madagascar’s sapphire market reportedly controlled by Sri Lankans and extensive smuggling documented</cite>.

Diamonds: concentrated supply, certification, and enforced scarcity
Early diamond supply concentration enabled stockpiling and coordinated scarcity. De Beers’ vertically integrated production and selective auctioning allowed it to direct supply to highest-value uses and sustain monopoly rents, even as the formal global monopolist declined <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">De Beers operates a large family of companies creating a near-monopoly and historically forced many independent sellers out of business</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-1">De Beers sold only to handpicked dealers and relied on sightholders to route rough stones to most valuable uses, sustaining a pricing strategy that preserved downstream rents</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-2">As De Beers’ share declined to ~35% by value, prices per carat rose and margins stayed high, consistent with oligopolistic mimicry of monopoly behavior</cite>. Operationally, De Beers’ London-based DTC auctions tied buyers to a narrow set of channels, while strategic reserves and timing enabled artificial scarcity and price control <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">De Beers’ DTC conducted auctions ten times a year, using stocked diamonds to create artificial scarcity and manipulate prices</cite>.

The Kimberley Process Certification Scheme (KPCS) provided an international trade regime that could be enforced at borders and penalized conflict-affected shipments, complementing producer-side supply management. Although imperfect, its sanctions created credible downside risks for exporting conflict-affected rough <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">The UN in 1998 imposed an embargo on rough diamonds from Angola without official certificates, and NGOs exposed widespread sanctions violations in UNITA-linked trade, catalyzing a broader response</cite>. Still, enforcement gaps and loopholes—such as allowing “mixed” sources without traceability—undermined effectiveness, especially where state capacity is weak and producers like De Beers could obscure origins <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">De Beers labeled sources as “mixed” without clear proof, and Kimberley enforcement relied on participants instituting quality checks that could definitively establish origin, which many resisted</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-3">Many scholars argue Kimberley should require granular “footprints” via lab analysis to prevent smuggling and misdeclaration; without it, the scheme remains vulnerable</cite>. Importantly, even with these flaws, certification plus concentrated supply and chokepoint hubs (e.g., Antwerp, New York) allowed scarcity signals to travel and deter diversion, stabilizing prices <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">Belgium’s role as a world diamond trade hub (AWDC) and De Beers’ control over supply enabled centralized pricing power and stock control</cite>.

Colored gemstones: fragmented supply chains, heterogeneous value, and porous borders
Colored gemstone supply is geographically dispersed across many artisanal mines and small-scale operations, with heterogeneous qualities where value per carat swings sharply with color, clarity, cut, and origin. This multiplicity prevents a single certifier from credibly constraining supply-wide scarcity and origin claims <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Stones vary widely in value per carat depending on scarcity, quality, and origin; the value chain mixes many artisanal mines and traders; and informal transactions limit transparency</cite>. Trade then funnels through porous, low-regulation corridors and hubs—Bangkok, Sri Lanka, Malawi, Tanzania—where smuggling and rebranding are routine and hard to police, erasing certification advantages at borders <cite id="21e8bf0f-0">Colored gemstones are smuggled out of Mozambique through Malawi and Tanzania or directly from airports in Nampula and Pemba to Thailand/Sri Lanka; VIP lounges are used for smuggling; Thai and Sri Lankan buyers dominate parts of the ruby trade</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-3">African sapphires are rebranded as “Ceylon sapphires” in Sri Lanka, with smuggling networks controlling a large share of Madagascar’s sapphire trade and significant fraud reported</cite>. Because buyers cannot reliably verify origin or treatment and because much trade is informal, demand-side price signals cannot be credibly manipulated into a systemic scarcity narrative without a credible, enforced provenance regime <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Lack of transparency in informal, heterogeneous value chains makes end customers wary of unethical or harmful upstream practices and creates challenges for ethical standards</cite>.

Certification and provenance systems for colored gems are fragmented and still evolving, limiting the disciplining power of certification. While initiatives like GIA, AGL, IGI, and HGI exist, their standards and acceptance vary, and cross-border enforcement is uneven. Efforts to digitize provenance (e.g., Everledger/Gübelin) show promise by creating tamper-resistant digital twins and role-based uploads, but adoption across the fragmented value chain remains limited and uneven relative to the diamond sector’s homogenized KPCS <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Transactions rely on trust and reputation; a large volume is informal with limited transparency; Gübelin Gem Lab and Everledger introduced a blockchain “Provenance Proof” to create digital twins and store attributes along the chain</cite>. In contrast, the Kimberley Process, despite its enforcement limits, created a near-universal export/import framework with punitive sanctions that can discipline state-linked smuggling in conflict-affected regions, albeit imperfectly <cite id="0ce1ea95-3">Kimberley relies on voluntary compliance; without stronger enforcement and origin verification, smuggling and misdeclaration remain effective loopholes</cite>.

Supply substitutability and competitive origins blunt scarcity signals
Colored gemstones have many competitive sources and attributes, so increases in supply from new or expanding mines (e.g., Madagascar for rubies/sapphires) or improved recovery/processing rapidly dilute scarcity claims and compress prices <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">Diamonds are most plentiful in nations with weak governments, where internal controls are limited and smuggling hampers enforcement; in contrast, many colored gem regions have artisanal sectors and porous borders</cite> <cite id="7a3c1a97-0">Ruby occurs in Madagascar, Mozambique, Myanmar, Tanzania, Thailand; Madagascar has developed as an important new source as Asian production declined, increasing supply</cite>. Quality heterogeneity means only a subset of material commands premium prices (e.g., Kashmir sapphires), so scarcity cannot be generalized across grades or origins; certification must distinguish attributes precisely, which the colored-gem sector has only partially standardized <cite id="7a3c1a97-0">Sapphire from Kashmir commands some of the highest prices; ethical concerns include undisclosed “doctoring” of lower-quality gemstones, underscoring variability and treatment opacity</cite>. By contrast, diamonds’ largely homogeneous valuation criteria (4Cs analogs) and centralized trade hubs make certification signals more potent and easier to police at borders <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">Diamonds’ distinctive “footprint” in lab analysis suggests origin can be identified; strengthening Kimberley checks could curb smuggling</cite>.

Gray-market flows and rebranding erode certification power
In colored gems, smuggling is not just about volume but also about rebranding low-value material into high-value provenance narratives (e.g., Africa→Sri Lanka→“Ceylon” rubies/sapphires), which undermines price supports and devalues certified seals <cite id="21e8bf0f-3">Sapphires from Africa are often smuggled to Sri Lanka and sold as “Ceylon sapphires,” with about 70% of Madagascar’s market reportedly controlled by Sri Lankans and significant smuggling and fraud documented</cite>. These practices exploit fragmented regulation and weak customs capacity, particularly in source countries and transit hubs, which the Kimberley framework did not fully close in diamonds and which are far worse in colored gems due to greater supply diversity and less concentrated chokepoints <cite id="21e8bf0f-0">VIP airport lounges in Mozambique’s Nampula and Pemba are used for smuggling colored gemstones; Lilongwe is a major conduit; Thai and Sri Lankan buyers are prominent smugglers in the ruby trade</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-2">In Pakistan, the absence of official regulatory environment and customs extortion at airports constrains legitimate trade and highlights how weak governance undermines gemstone business</cite>.

Demand-side price sensitivity and policy shocks
Colored gem prices are highly sensitive to supply-demand balance, with empirical models showing price increases when supply is tight and decreases when supply rises or demand falls; external shocks (macro, FX, policy) also propagate quickly through heterogeneous channels <cite id="8fdce0c7-0">Ruby price changes impact the jewelry market; when supply decreases or demand increases, prices may rise; stability is crucial; large fluctuations raise uncertainty and affect consumer purchasing</cite> <cite id="8fdce0c7-3">If supply exceeds demand, competition increases and prices fall; if supply is insufficient, prices may rise; market stability reduces volatility and shapes expectations</cite>. Because demand reacts to price and perceived value, attempts to enforce artificial scarcity without credible provenance and widespread compliance tend to collapse under smuggling and substitution, whereas in diamonds, the combination of concentration and certification created a durable illusion of scarcity that buyers trusted at retail <cite id="0ce1ea95-2">Even as production became more competitive, average prices per carat rose and margins stayed high, indicating that buyers and sellers accepted oligopolistic scarcity signals</cite>.

Case evidence: policy attempts and outcomes
Targeted export bans and certification in conflict zones have had mixed and often temporary effects in colored gems. The UN’s 1998 embargo on Angolan rough (initially triggered by UNITA-linked trade) exposed how smuggling and opaque trade networks nullified sanctions, prompting the Kimberley framework; yet similar blanket measures in colored gems (e.g., bans on Burmese rubies/sapphires) have struggled with parallel trade, rebranding, and demand substitution, while certification initiatives remain fragmented and adoption uneven <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">The UN embargo on Angola without certificates was violated massively, leading to broader efforts to curb conflict diamonds; however, state capacity and parallel trade networks undermine sanctions</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-3">Smuggling and rebranding of African sapphires into “Ceylon” stones demonstrates how certification labels can be circumvented at major hubs</cite>. In contrast, diamonds’ centralized auctions, homogenized standards, and stronger enforcement at major hubs allowed scarcity-backed price supports to persist despite known loopholes and political exceptions <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">De Beers’ ability to label origins as “mixed” and the Kimberley system’s reliance on participant quality checks expose the limits of current enforcement</cite>.

Synthesis: why scarcity control succeeded in diamonds but not colored gems
- Concentration and chokepoints: De Beers/DTC’s auctioned oligopoly plus Antwerp/NY hubs gave centralized control over timing, allocation, and signaling of scarcity; diamonds’ value depends less on origin than on universally recognized quality metrics, making certification and grading more uniform <cite id="0ce1ea95-1">De Beers’ strategy relied on sightholders to route rough to highest value, sustaining a pricing regime</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-2">Producer margins and prices stayed high even as share declined, consistent with effective scarcity control</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">Diamonds’ distinctive “footprint” allows origin verification to deter smuggling</cite>.
- Fragmented supply and heterogeneity in colored gems: Many artisanal mines, variable quality, and multiple geographies prevent a single authority from credibly constraining supply-wide scarcity; value varies by origin and treatment, complicating universal grading standards <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Heterogeneous value chains, informal transactions, and lack of transparency raise ethical and pricing challenges</cite>.
- Enforcement and smuggling: Kimberley-style sanctions and border checks deter some conflict-rough flows, but colored gems’ porous borders, airport smuggling corridors, and rebranding networks largely neutralize certification at points of sale and transit <cite id="21e8bf0f-0">Colored gem smuggling routes via Malawi/Tanzania and airport VIP lounges are well-documented</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-3">Rebranding African sapphires as “Ceylon” sapphires is widespread and profitable</cite>.
- Substitutability and competitive entry: New sources (e.g., Madagascar) and improved recovery quickly expand supply for rubies/sapphires, compressing prices and undermining scarcity claims, whereas diamond supply additions are rarer and coordinated to a greater extent via DTC stockpiles and timing <cite id="7a3c1a97-0">Madagascar has emerged as an important ruby source as Asian production declined, increasing supply</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">De Beers historically used stockpiled rough to manage scarcity through controlled auctions</cite>.
- Evolving certification infrastructure: Blockchain-based provenance (e.g., Everledger/Gübelin) is promising but remains unevenly adopted; diamond certification is more homogenized, giving certification more disciplining power <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Gübelin and Everledger created digital twins and role-based data uploads to improve provenance, but adoption hinges on trust and transparency across heterogeneous actors</cite>.

Policy implications and outlook
For colored gemstones, credible artificial scarcity would require: universal, tamper-resistant provenance at origin; harmonized grading/treatment disclosure recognized across major hubs; and enforcement at ports/airlines with credible sanctions and customs capacity, coupled with traceable supply-chain finance and insurance to reduce informal channels <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Complexity and informality create barriers to financing and ethical standards; digital provenance can store dimensions, color, cut, and treatment to build trust</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-0">Airport and border smuggling corridors demand customs and hub-level enforcement reforms</cite>. In diamonds, incremental improvements to Kimberley (mandatory granular origin “footprints,” stronger penalties, and reduced exceptions for opaque “mixed” sources) could narrow but not eliminate smuggling and political carve-outs, suggesting a ceiling to certification-only approaches <cite id="0ce1ea95-3">Mandating granular origin analysis and closing smuggling loopholes would require participants to sever ties with opaque supply, which remains politically difficult</cite>. As synthetic and lab-grown colored gems grow, demand-side substitution pressures will further test the durability of any artificial scarcity; transparency on treatment and origin becomes even more essential to maintain differentiated value tiers <cite id="7a3c1a97-1">Ethical concerns include undisclosed “doctoring” of lower-quality gemstones, underscoring the premium on truthful treatment disclosure</cite>.

What would resolve remaining uncertainty
- Head-to-head elasticity experiments under comparable certification: randomized audits comparing price and volume under uniform KPCS-like certification vs. fragmented color-origin-specific seals across colored gems.
- Adoption and traceability trials: pilot universal digital twin provenance across key corridors (e.g., Mozambique→Thailand, Colombia→U.S.) with enforced customs checks to measure smuggling compression and price stabilization.
- Synthetic disclosure mandates: standardized lab-grown vs. natural labeling and origin disclosure to isolate the effect of transparency on price tiers and demand.

In short, diamond scarcity control worked because supply was concentrated, certification homogenized quality and origin signals, and chokepoint enforcement was credible enough to deter smuggling and sustain price supports; colored gemstones lack these preconditions—fragmented supply and grading, porous borders, and abundant substitutes make centralized artificial scarcity self-defeating absent deeper, universal compliance and provenance infrastructure <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">Diamonds’ vertical integration, selective auctions, and distinctive “footprint” underpinned artificial scarcity</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-2">Oligopolistic pricing and margins persisted despite reduced De Beers share, indicating effective scarcity</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Colored gemstone trade’s complexity and informality impede universal certification and enforcement</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-0">Documented smuggling routes and airport facilitation expose structural vulnerabilities</cite>.

The motives and practices of De Beers are highly questionable, especially considering the preferential treatment the group enjoys from the Kimberley Process Certification Scheme. The Kimberley Process does not require De Beers to mention the sources of their gemstones. Bhaskar [3] explains that, "this group labels the source as being 'mixed', without any clear proof of origin." Although De Beers operates their own mines throughout Africa, the true origins of their on the market are completely unknown. This practice is contrary to the mission of the Kimberley Process and undermines the spirit of the certification scheme. 

Yet another problem with the Kimberley Process deals with the regions in which diamonds are mined. Diamonds are most plentiful in nations such as Zimbabwe (as previously mentioned), the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sierra Leone, and Angola. These nations all had violent wars within the past few decades. These struggles left them with weak governments and few internal controls to regulate the diamond trade. As Smilie conveys to Melik [12], the Kimberley Process is severely disadvantaged in nations with already lax gem management. Smilie explains the situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, saying, "the government in Congo has no idea where 40% of its diamonds come from -they could be coming from Angola or Zimbabwe or even from Mars" [12]. When conflict diamonds are smuggled, the governments cannot effectively trace them back to their true origins, instead passing them off as mined cleanly. 

Enforcement is a key issue preventing the effectiveness of the Kimberley Process Certification Scheme. However, the participants could easily institute quality checks that definitively provide the true origin of the diamond. Bhaskar [3] explains that every diamond has a distinctive "footprint."
