In fact, De Beers' vertically integrated strategies help explain some curiosities of the prior strategy. Economic theory implies that an upstream monopolist maximizes profit when downstream markets are competitive. Yet De Beers, in contrast to theory, sold only to handpicked dealers. Moreover, and similarly in contrast to theory, diamond merchants have clamored to become a sightholder atop the distribution stream, which suggests that De Beers sells diamonds to sightholders at less than the monopoly price and instead shares with them some monopoly rents. The reason for De Beers' curious distribution strategy is that it relied on these merchants to ensure that rough stones were directed to their most valuable use. It therefore selected as sightholders merchants who were deeply familiar with the diamond trade to know how to cut, distribute, and market diamonds to create maximum value. In short, De Beers relied on downstream merchants' market information and industry expertise, and the company implemented a pricing strategy that economically sustained these knowledgeable intermediaries.

The industry's longtime intermediaries-especially mid-size and small operators who do not partner with leading retail chains-are both the primary victims of this new pricing strategy and the most vulnerable. Compared with the upstream production and downstream retail markets, this intermediate market for distributing and cutting rough diamonds has long offered the slimmest margins (see Figure 5), and producers' pricing efforts have caused these margins to continue to shrink. Consequently, De Beers' new strategy has had major reverberations throughout the diamond distribution chain.

Snippet: Industry: The colored gemstone industry reveals three peculiarities. First, the stones vary largely in their value per carat, depending on the characteristics of the stone, such as scarcity, quality, origin, and customer attractiveness. Hence, assessing the characteristics of a stone is key for evaluating the value of a colored gemstone. Second, the value chain in the colored gemstone industry is highly complex and heterogeneous. There are many artisanal mines and only a few large-scale mines with heavy machinery on the mining stage. These are followed by traders that have either a regional, national, or international customer networks, refiners with diverse specializations in terms of cut and treatment, exporters, regional, national, and international wholesalers, jewelers, and retail brands [18]. Third, the transactions within the industry are based on mutual trust and reputation between transaction partners (e.g., miners and regional traders). A large volume of the trade is informal with limited transparency for external parties, causing substantial challenges for financing, insurance, and ethical standards. The previously described three peculiarities turned into a burden given the lack of transparency in the industry. First, for end-customers or upstream actors (e.g., retail brands), the actions of previous stages in the value chain are not transparent given the complexity and heterogeneity of the value chain as well as the informal transactions. Hence, buyers fear to finance unethical or ecological harmful actions in the downstream value chain. Second, end-customer as layperson having a hard time assessing the characteristics of a stone and its value. Consequently, end-customers are expecting more transparency on aspects such as origin, authenticity, and physical qualities. 

Blockchain application: Against this backdrop, Gübelin Gem Lab1 and Everledger2 introduced the Provenance Proof Blockchain3 for the colored gemstone industry. The blockchain solutions allow creating a digital twin for each colored gemstone and storing all relevant information (e.g., physical dimensions, color, cut) along the value chain. Each stage in the value chain has its own role and enables to upload of role-specific information.

Title: Problems Faced by Online Gemstone Traders of NamakMandi market at Pakistani Airports
Snippet: Purpose: This paper analyses the views and experiences of gemstone traders at the NamakMandi (NM) gemstone market. 
Methodology: The paper draws on the data from a stakeholder’s workshop held at Bacha Khan University Charsadda (Pakistan) and ten (10) semi-structured interviews primarily with traders, which were conducted as part of a larger research project for identifying factors inhibiting the beneficiation of gemstones in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan. 
Findings: The paper demonstrates that while the advent of the internet has ushered in quite a new era in the gemstone trade, particularly triggering higher interest among youth to initiate online gemstone businesses, but they are improvising and experimenting in an environment that is completely devoid of any official regulatory environment or support. In the face of the absence of relevant laws and regulations, the employees of the customs department at the airport resort to extortions and bribes both during the exportation and importation of gemstones in Pakistan. 
Implications: Unless an appropriate regulatory and supportive environment is created, online gemstone businesses may have a very sluggish growth, thus, taping its potential to create income-earning opportunities and revenue for the government.

Title: Zimbabwe's coloured gemstone endowments - A regional geological overview
Snippet: A gemstone is a mineral, rock, or other material that is prized for its beauty, durability, and rarity. Coloured gemstones are gemstones other than diamond (GIA, 1999); an alternative definition to the older subdivision that recognized precious (superior) versus semi-precious (inferior) gemstones (GIA, 1999;Lurie, 2000). Diamond, emerald, ruby, sapphire, and pearls were considered precious and the rest of the gemstones such as amethyst, tourmaline, aquamarine, citrine, and garnet were designated semi-precious (Lurie 2000). In the newer, preferred GIA (1999) definition, gemstones other than diamond include amber, ivory, and coral, which are organic materials (GIA, 1999;Lurie, 2000), thus gemstones need not necessarily be inorganic and crystalline. 

Although Zimbabwe has a significant gemstone endowment, the country is better known for its platinum group metals, chromite, gold, diamond, and coal resources (Bartholomew 1990). There is less awareness of the country's non-diamond (coloured) gemstone endowment. A notable exception is the global acclaim of the exquisite green Sandawana emeralds, discovered in 1956(Tyndale-Biscoe, 1968; Bartholomew, 1990), which firmly established the country as one of the emerald capitals of the world. Zimbabwean aquamarine and alexandrite have also earned global recognition, and are mentioned in international general gemmology textbooks such as Cipriani and Borelli (1986) and Read (2005). Other coloured gemstones, including amethyst, ruby, sapphire, tourmaline, garnet, citrine, and iolite, are regarded as the lesser known gemstones of Zimbabwe. Most classes of coloured gemstones, but particularly these lesser known examples, have received only cursory scientific and industrial attention. For example, a search on Scopus using keywords Zimbabwe AND gemstones returns only four results, whereas a search for Zimbabwe AND pegmatites (a major gemstone host lithology) returns 32 results -most focusing on the economically important Bikita, Kamativi, and Sandawana pegmatites.

Title: Dynamic Analysis of Ruby Price Changes on Future Trends in the Jewelry Market Based on Genetic Algorithm Model
Snippet: : As a precious gemstone, ruby's price fluctuations have an important impact on the jewelry market. However, accurate analysis of ruby price trends and their impact on the future of the jewelry market has been difficult. This article aims to reveal the impact mechanism of ruby price changes on the future trend of the jewelry market through dynamic analysis based on a genetic algorithm model. To achieve this goal, we collected relevant data including supply and demand data, market stability indicators, changes in consumer demand and external factors, and applied genetic algorithm models for analysis. Through the analysis of data and the operation of the model, this article has obtained the trend prediction of ruby prices and the impact of price changes on the jewelry market. The contribution of this study is to provide a dynamic analysis method based on a genetic algorithm model, which can more accurately predict the trend of ruby prices, and provide an in-depth analysis of the factors affecting the price changes on the jewelry market. These research results provide important references for practitioners in the jewelry industry, allowing them to better understand market dynamics and make appropriate decisions. At the same time, this study also provides reference and inspiration for future research on dynamic analysis of trends in the jewelry market.

Below is a synthesis of why artificial supply restrictions have historically stabilized prices and allocation in the diamond market but have not produced the same systemic effects in colored gemstone markets. The explanation emphasizes market structure, certification and enforcement, supply-side substitutability, and smuggling/gray-market dynamics, with concrete examples and mechanisms.

Summary of the contrast
Artificial supply restriction has “worked” in diamonds because a few vertically integrated producers controlled early supply, coupled with a credible Kimberley Process-style certification and trade chokepoints that let a cartel-like oligopoly enforce scarcity and deter smuggling, keeping rough prices stable even as the formal monopoly eroded <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">De Beers historically dominated diamond sales and used selective selling and stockpiling to create artificial scarcity and manipulate prices</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">With stocked diamonds, De Beers was able to create an artificial scarcity that allowed it to manipulate the price of diamonds around the world</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-2">Despite De Beers’ market share decline to roughly a third by value, average rough/polished prices per carat have increased and producer margins remained high, indicating retained monopolistic features</cite>. By contrast, colored gemstones are produced by many artisanal and small-scale miners in numerous geographies with heterogeneous qualities and low-cost processing hubs, fragmented certification, and high smuggling and rebranding fraud, undermining any centralized scarcity regime <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">The colored gemstone value chain is highly complex and heterogeneous, with many artisanal mines and informal transactions that limit transparency</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-3">Sapphires from Africa are often smuggled to Sri Lanka and sold as “Ceylon sapphires,” with about 70% of Madagascar’s sapphire market reportedly controlled by Sri Lankans and extensive smuggling documented</cite>.

Diamonds: concentrated supply, certification, and enforced scarcity
Early diamond supply concentration enabled stockpiling and coordinated scarcity. De Beers’ vertically integrated production and selective auctioning allowed it to direct supply to highest-value uses and sustain monopoly rents, even as the formal global monopolist declined <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">De Beers operates a large family of companies creating a near-monopoly and historically forced many independent sellers out of business</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-1">De Beers sold only to handpicked dealers and relied on sightholders to route rough stones to most valuable uses, sustaining a pricing strategy that preserved downstream rents</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-2">As De Beers’ share declined to ~35% by value, prices per carat rose and margins stayed high, consistent with oligopolistic mimicry of monopoly behavior</cite>. Operationally, De Beers’ London-based DTC auctions tied buyers to a narrow set of channels, while strategic reserves and timing enabled artificial scarcity and price control <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">De Beers’ DTC conducted auctions ten times a year, using stocked diamonds to create artificial scarcity and manipulate prices</cite>.

The Kimberley Process Certification Scheme (KPCS) provided an international trade regime that could be enforced at borders and penalized conflict-affected shipments, complementing producer-side supply management. Although imperfect, its sanctions created credible downside risks for exporting conflict-affected rough <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">The UN in 1998 imposed an embargo on rough diamonds from Angola without official certificates, and NGOs exposed widespread sanctions violations in UNITA-linked trade, catalyzing a broader response</cite>. Still, enforcement gaps and loopholes—such as allowing “mixed” sources without traceability—undermined effectiveness, especially where state capacity is weak and producers like De Beers could obscure origins <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">De Beers labeled sources as “mixed” without clear proof, and Kimberley enforcement relied on participants instituting quality checks that could definitively establish origin, which many resisted</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-3">Many scholars argue Kimberley should require granular “footprints” via lab analysis to prevent smuggling and misdeclaration; without it, the scheme remains vulnerable</cite>. Importantly, even with these flaws, certification plus concentrated supply and chokepoint hubs (e.g., Antwerp, New York) allowed scarcity signals to travel and deter diversion, stabilizing prices <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">Belgium’s role as a world diamond trade hub (AWDC) and De Beers’ control over supply enabled centralized pricing power and stock control</cite>.

Colored gemstones: fragmented supply chains, heterogeneous value, and porous borders
Colored gemstone supply is geographically dispersed across many artisanal mines and small-scale operations, with heterogeneous qualities where value per carat swings sharply with color, clarity, cut, and origin. This multiplicity prevents a single certifier from credibly constraining supply-wide scarcity and origin claims <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Stones vary widely in value per carat depending on scarcity, quality, and origin; the value chain mixes many artisanal mines and traders; and informal transactions limit transparency</cite>. Trade then funnels through porous, low-regulation corridors and hubs—Bangkok, Sri Lanka, Malawi, Tanzania—where smuggling and rebranding are routine and hard to police, erasing certification advantages at borders <cite id="21e8bf0f-0">Colored gemstones are smuggled out of Mozambique through Malawi and Tanzania or directly from airports in Nampula and Pemba to Thailand/Sri Lanka; VIP lounges are used for smuggling; Thai and Sri Lankan buyers dominate parts of the ruby trade</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-3">African sapphires are rebranded as “Ceylon sapphires” in Sri Lanka, with smuggling networks controlling a large share of Madagascar’s sapphire trade and significant fraud reported</cite>. Because buyers cannot reliably verify origin or treatment and because much trade is informal, demand-side price signals cannot be credibly manipulated into a systemic scarcity narrative without a credible, enforced provenance regime <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Lack of transparency in informal, heterogeneous value chains makes end customers wary of unethical or harmful upstream practices and creates challenges for ethical standards</cite>.

Certification and provenance systems for colored gems are fragmented and still evolving, limiting the disciplining power of certification. While initiatives like GIA, AGL, IGI, and HGI exist, their standards and acceptance vary, and cross-border enforcement is uneven. Efforts to digitize provenance (e.g., Everledger/Gübelin) show promise by creating tamper-resistant digital twins and role-based uploads, but adoption across the fragmented value chain remains limited and uneven relative to the diamond sector’s homogenized KPCS <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Transactions rely on trust and reputation; a large volume is informal with limited transparency; Gübelin Gem Lab and Everledger introduced a blockchain “Provenance Proof” to create digital twins and store attributes along the chain</cite>. In contrast, the Kimberley Process, despite its enforcement limits, created a near-universal export/import framework with punitive sanctions that can discipline state-linked smuggling in conflict-affected regions, albeit imperfectly <cite id="0ce1ea95-3">Kimberley relies on voluntary compliance; without stronger enforcement and origin verification, smuggling and misdeclaration remain effective loopholes</cite>.

Supply substitutability and competitive origins blunt scarcity signals
Colored gemstones have many competitive sources and attributes, so increases in supply from new or expanding mines (e.g., Madagascar for rubies/sapphires) or improved recovery/processing rapidly dilute scarcity claims and compress prices <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">Diamonds are most plentiful in nations with weak governments, where internal controls are limited and smuggling hampers enforcement; in contrast, many colored gem regions have artisanal sectors and porous borders</cite> <cite id="7a3c1a97-0">Ruby occurs in Madagascar, Mozambique, Myanmar, Tanzania, Thailand; Madagascar has developed as an important new source as Asian production declined, increasing supply</cite>. Quality heterogeneity means only a subset of material commands premium prices (e.g., Kashmir sapphires), so scarcity cannot be generalized across grades or origins; certification must distinguish attributes precisely, which the colored-gem sector has only partially standardized <cite id="7a3c1a97-0">Sapphire from Kashmir commands some of the highest prices; ethical concerns include undisclosed “doctoring” of lower-quality gemstones, underscoring variability and treatment opacity</cite>. By contrast, diamonds’ largely homogeneous valuation criteria (4Cs analogs) and centralized trade hubs make certification signals more potent and easier to police at borders <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">Diamonds’ distinctive “footprint” in lab analysis suggests origin can be identified; strengthening Kimberley checks could curb smuggling</cite>.

Gray-market flows and rebranding erode certification power
In colored gems, smuggling is not just about volume but also about rebranding low-value material into high-value provenance narratives (e.g., Africa→Sri Lanka→“Ceylon” rubies/sapphires), which undermines price supports and devalues certified seals <cite id="21e8bf0f-3">Sapphires from Africa are often smuggled to Sri Lanka and sold as “Ceylon sapphires,” with about 70% of Madagascar’s market reportedly controlled by Sri Lankans and significant smuggling and fraud documented</cite>. These practices exploit fragmented regulation and weak customs capacity, particularly in source countries and transit hubs, which the Kimberley framework did not fully close in diamonds and which are far worse in colored gems due to greater supply diversity and less concentrated chokepoints <cite id="21e8bf0f-0">VIP airport lounges in Mozambique’s Nampula and Pemba are used for smuggling colored gemstones; Lilongwe is a major conduit; Thai and Sri Lankan buyers are prominent smugglers in the ruby trade</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-2">In Pakistan, the absence of official regulatory environment and customs extortion at airports constrains legitimate trade and highlights how weak governance undermines gemstone business</cite>.

Demand-side price sensitivity and policy shocks
Colored gem prices are highly sensitive to supply-demand balance, with empirical models showing price increases when supply is tight and decreases when supply rises or demand falls; external shocks (macro, FX, policy) also propagate quickly through heterogeneous channels <cite id="8fdce0c7-0">Ruby price changes impact the jewelry market; when supply decreases or demand increases, prices may rise; stability is crucial; large fluctuations raise uncertainty and affect consumer purchasing</cite> <cite id="8fdce0c7-3">If supply exceeds demand, competition increases and prices fall; if supply is insufficient, prices may rise; market stability reduces volatility and shapes expectations</cite>. Because demand reacts to price and perceived value, attempts to enforce artificial scarcity without credible provenance and widespread compliance tend to collapse under smuggling and substitution, whereas in diamonds, the combination of concentration and certification created a durable illusion of scarcity that buyers trusted at retail <cite id="0ce1ea95-2">Even as production became more competitive, average prices per carat rose and margins stayed high, indicating that buyers and sellers accepted oligopolistic scarcity signals</cite>.

Case evidence: policy attempts and outcomes
Targeted export bans and certification in conflict zones have had mixed and often temporary effects in colored gems. The UN’s 1998 embargo on Angolan rough (initially triggered by UNITA-linked trade) exposed how smuggling and opaque trade networks nullified sanctions, prompting the Kimberley framework; yet similar blanket measures in colored gems (e.g., bans on Burmese rubies/sapphires) have struggled with parallel trade, rebranding, and demand substitution, while certification initiatives remain fragmented and adoption uneven <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">The UN embargo on Angola without certificates was violated massively, leading to broader efforts to curb conflict diamonds; however, state capacity and parallel trade networks undermine sanctions</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-3">Smuggling and rebranding of African sapphires into “Ceylon” stones demonstrates how certification labels can be circumvented at major hubs</cite>. In contrast, diamonds’ centralized auctions, homogenized standards, and stronger enforcement at major hubs allowed scarcity-backed price supports to persist despite known loopholes and political exceptions <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">De Beers’ ability to label origins as “mixed” and the Kimberley system’s reliance on participant quality checks expose the limits of current enforcement</cite>.

Synthesis: why scarcity control succeeded in diamonds but not colored gems
- Concentration and chokepoints: De Beers/DTC’s auctioned oligopoly plus Antwerp/NY hubs gave centralized control over timing, allocation, and signaling of scarcity; diamonds’ value depends less on origin than on universally recognized quality metrics, making certification and grading more uniform <cite id="0ce1ea95-1">De Beers’ strategy relied on sightholders to route rough to highest value, sustaining a pricing regime</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-2">Producer margins and prices stayed high even as share declined, consistent with effective scarcity control</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">Diamonds’ distinctive “footprint” allows origin verification to deter smuggling</cite>.
- Fragmented supply and heterogeneity in colored gems: Many artisanal mines, variable quality, and multiple geographies prevent a single authority from credibly constraining supply-wide scarcity; value varies by origin and treatment, complicating universal grading standards <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Heterogeneous value chains, informal transactions, and lack of transparency raise ethical and pricing challenges</cite>.
- Enforcement and smuggling: Kimberley-style sanctions and border checks deter some conflict-rough flows, but colored gems’ porous borders, airport smuggling corridors, and rebranding networks largely neutralize certification at points of sale and transit <cite id="21e8bf0f-0">Colored gem smuggling routes via Malawi/Tanzania and airport VIP lounges are well-documented</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-3">Rebranding African sapphires as “Ceylon” sapphires is widespread and profitable</cite>.
- Substitutability and competitive entry: New sources (e.g., Madagascar) and improved recovery quickly expand supply for rubies/sapphires, compressing prices and undermining scarcity claims, whereas diamond supply additions are rarer and coordinated to a greater extent via DTC stockpiles and timing <cite id="7a3c1a97-0">Madagascar has emerged as an important ruby source as Asian production declined, increasing supply</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-4">De Beers historically used stockpiled rough to manage scarcity through controlled auctions</cite>.
- Evolving certification infrastructure: Blockchain-based provenance (e.g., Everledger/Gübelin) is promising but remains unevenly adopted; diamond certification is more homogenized, giving certification more disciplining power <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Gübelin and Everledger created digital twins and role-based data uploads to improve provenance, but adoption hinges on trust and transparency across heterogeneous actors</cite>.

Policy implications and outlook
For colored gemstones, credible artificial scarcity would require: universal, tamper-resistant provenance at origin; harmonized grading/treatment disclosure recognized across major hubs; and enforcement at ports/airlines with credible sanctions and customs capacity, coupled with traceable supply-chain finance and insurance to reduce informal channels <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Complexity and informality create barriers to financing and ethical standards; digital provenance can store dimensions, color, cut, and treatment to build trust</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-0">Airport and border smuggling corridors demand customs and hub-level enforcement reforms</cite>. In diamonds, incremental improvements to Kimberley (mandatory granular origin “footprints,” stronger penalties, and reduced exceptions for opaque “mixed” sources) could narrow but not eliminate smuggling and political carve-outs, suggesting a ceiling to certification-only approaches <cite id="0ce1ea95-3">Mandating granular origin analysis and closing smuggling loopholes would require participants to sever ties with opaque supply, which remains politically difficult</cite>. As synthetic and lab-grown colored gems grow, demand-side substitution pressures will further test the durability of any artificial scarcity; transparency on treatment and origin becomes even more essential to maintain differentiated value tiers <cite id="7a3c1a97-1">Ethical concerns include undisclosed “doctoring” of lower-quality gemstones, underscoring the premium on truthful treatment disclosure</cite>.

What would resolve remaining uncertainty
- Head-to-head elasticity experiments under comparable certification: randomized audits comparing price and volume under uniform KPCS-like certification vs. fragmented color-origin-specific seals across colored gems.
- Adoption and traceability trials: pilot universal digital twin provenance across key corridors (e.g., Mozambique→Thailand, Colombia→U.S.) with enforced customs checks to measure smuggling compression and price stabilization.
- Synthetic disclosure mandates: standardized lab-grown vs. natural labeling and origin disclosure to isolate the effect of transparency on price tiers and demand.

In short, diamond scarcity control worked because supply was concentrated, certification homogenized quality and origin signals, and chokepoint enforcement was credible enough to deter smuggling and sustain price supports; colored gemstones lack these preconditions—fragmented supply and grading, porous borders, and abundant substitutes make centralized artificial scarcity self-defeating absent deeper, universal compliance and provenance infrastructure <cite id="0ce1ea95-0">Diamonds’ vertical integration, selective auctions, and distinctive “footprint” underpinned artificial scarcity</cite> <cite id="0ce1ea95-2">Oligopolistic pricing and margins persisted despite reduced De Beers share, indicating effective scarcity</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-1">Colored gemstone trade’s complexity and informality impede universal certification and enforcement</cite> <cite id="21e8bf0f-0">Documented smuggling routes and airport facilitation expose structural vulnerabilities</cite>.</answer>

In fact, De Beers' vertically integrated strategies help explain some curiosities of the prior strategy. Economic theory implies that an upstream monopolist maximizes profit when downstream markets are competitive. Yet De Beers, in contrast to theory, sold only to handpicked dealers. Moreover, and similarly in contrast to theory, diamond merchants have clamored to become a sightholder atop the distribution stream, which suggests that De Beers sells diamonds to sightholders at less than the monopoly price and instead shares with them some monopoly rents. The reason for De Beers' curious distribution strategy is that it relied on these merchants to ensure that rough stones were directed to their most valuable use. It therefore selected as sightholders merchants who were deeply familiar with the diamond trade to know how to cut, distribute, and market diamonds to create maximum value. In short, De Beers relied on downstream merchants' market information and industry expertise, and the company implemented a pricing strategy that economically sustained these knowledgeable intermediaries.

The industry's longtime intermediaries-especially mid-size and small operators who do not partner with leading retail chains-are both the primary victims of this new pricing strategy and the most vulnerable. Compared with the upstream production and downstream retail markets, this intermediate market for distributing and cutting rough diamonds has long offered the slimmest margins (see Figure 5), and producers' pricing efforts have caused these margins to continue to shrink. Consequently, De Beers' new strategy has had major reverberations throughout the diamond distribution chain.

Snippet: Bhaskar [3] explains that every diamond has a distinctive "footprint." By analyzing the "granular structure of roughs", laboratories can identify the mines from which the gems originated. This practice would ensure that diamonds truly came from the regions that the sellers claim. Further, laboratory testing would prevent the sale of smuggled diamonds, which is one of the many loopholes of the Kimberley Process. 

However, many scholars, including Bhaskar [3], wonder why the Kimberley Process has not already instituted such a practice. The reasons trace back to the De Beers group and their interests. As previously mentioned, De Beers is not required to report the origins of their stones, leading many to believe that the company is engaging in unethical mining and purchasing, allowing the company to retain their control over the African diamond market. Bhaskar [3,www.dnaindia.com/money] states that, "by refusing to adopt such a technique, there is increasing discomfort that the Kimberley Process Certification Scheme route is being used to force African countries to adopt norms that are found acceptable to De Beers." Greater enforcement and control over the Kimberley Process Certification Scheme would require the membership to sever ties with De Beers, allowing for a more objective view of the diamond trade. 

With no international law in place, the Kimberley Process is the only vehicle that attempts to regulate the trade of diamonds. In a 2012 interview by , Dunnebacke, a staffer at Global Witness, eludes that if a country is deemed to be selling conflict diamonds, there is virtually no enforcement in place. The only repercussions a nation would face are sanctions placed on them by the Kimberley Process. In fact, De Beers' vertically integrated strategies help explain some curiosities of the prior strategy. Economic theory implies that an upstream monopolist maximizes profit when downstream markets are competitive. Yet De Beers, in contrast to theory, sold only to handpicked dealers. Moreover, and similarly in contrast to theory, diamond merchants have clamored to become a sightholder atop the distribution stream, which suggests that De Beers sells diamonds to sightholders at less than the monopoly price and instead shares with them some monopoly rents. The reason for De Beers' curious distribution strategy is that it relied on these merchants to ensure that rough stones were directed to their most valuable use. It therefore selected as sightholders merchants who were deeply familiar with the diamond trade to know how to cut, distribute, and market diamonds to create maximum value. In short, De Beers relied on downstream merchants' market information and industry expertise, and the company implemented a pricing strategy that economically sustained these knowledgeable intermediaries.

The industry's longtime intermediaries-especially mid-size and small operators who do not partner with leading retail chains-are both the primary victims of this new pricing strategy and the most vulnerable. Compared with the upstream production and downstream retail markets, this intermediate market for distributing and cutting rough diamonds has long offered the slimmest margins (see Figure 5), and producers' pricing efforts have caused these margins to continue to shrink. Consequently, De Beers' new strategy has had major reverberations throughout the diamond distribution chain.

Bhaskar [3] explains that every diamond has a distinctive "footprint." By analyzing the "granular structure of roughs", laboratories can identify the mines from which the gems originated. This practice would ensure that diamonds truly came from the regions that the sellers claim. Further, laboratory testing would prevent the sale of smuggled diamonds, which is one of the many loopholes of the Kimberley Process. 

However, many scholars, including Bhaskar [3], wonder why the Kimberley Process has not already instituted such a practice. The reasons trace back to the De Beers group and their interests. As previously mentioned, De Beers is not required to report the origins of their stones, leading many to believe that the company is engaging in unethical mining and purchasing, allowing the company to retain their control over the African diamond market. Bhaskar [3,www.dnaindia.com/money] states that, "by refusing to adopt such a technique, there is increasing discomfort that the Kimberley Process Certification Scheme route is being used to force African countries to adopt norms that are found acceptable to De Beers." Greater enforcement and control over the Kimberley Process Certification Scheme would require the membership to sever ties with De Beers, allowing for a more objective view of the diamond trade. 

With no international law in place, the Kimberley Process is the only vehicle that attempts to regulate the trade of diamonds. In a 2012 interview by , Dunnebacke, a staffer at Global Witness, eludes that if a country is deemed to be selling conflict diamonds, there is virtually no enforcement in place. The only repercussions a nation would face are sanctions placed on them by the Kimberley Process. As Zimbabwe showed the world during the Marange incident, threatening to sell diamonds on the illicit market is an effective strategy against the minor consequences used by the Kimberley Process officials. Mugabe's stern approach rendered the Kimberley Process helpless in the face of a threat. The Kimberley Process must create stricter, harsher punishments for nations and leaders who knowingly defy the parameters of the certification scheme. In an interview by www.reuters.com], Simon Ranier, chief executive of the British Jewelers' Association notes, "What is needed is an additional process that stops elected governments from using diamonds in conflict against their own people."

Title: Beyond Task-technology Fit: Exploring Network Value of Blockchain Technology Based on Two Supply Chain Cases
Snippet: Industry: The colored gemstone industry reveals three peculiarities. First, the stones vary largely in their value per carat, depending on the characteristics of the stone, such as scarcity, quality, origin, and customer attractiveness. Hence, assessing the characteristics of a stone is key for evaluating the value of a colored gemstone. Second, the value chain in the colored gemstone industry is highly complex and heterogeneous. There are many artisanal mines and only a few large-scale mines with heavy machinery on the mining stage. These are followed by traders that have either a regional, national, or international customer networks, refiners with diverse specializations in terms of cut and treatment, exporters, regional, national, and international wholesalers, jewelers, and retail brands [18]. Third, the transactions within the industry are based on mutual trust and reputation between transaction partners (e.g., miners and regional traders). A large volume of the trade is informal with limited transparency for external parties, causing substantial challenges for financing, insurance, and ethical standards. The previously described three peculiarities turned into a burden given the lack of transparency in the industry. First, for end-customers or upstream actors (e.g., retail brands), the actions of previous stages in the value chain are not transparent given the complexity and heterogeneity of the value chain as well as the informal transactions. Hence, buyers fear to finance unethical or ecological harmful actions in the downstream value chain. Second, end-customer as layperson having a hard time assessing the characteristics of a stone and its value. Consequently, end-customers are expecting more transparency on aspects such as origin, authenticity, and physical qualities. 

Blockchain application: Against this backdrop, Gübelin Gem Lab1 and Everledger2 introduced the Provenance Proof Blockchain3 for the colored gemstone industry. The blockchain solutions allow creating a digital twin for each colored gemstone and storing all relevant information (e.g., physical dimensions, color, cut) along the value chain. Each stage in the value chain has its own role and enables to upload of role-specific information.

Title: Problems Faced by Online Gemstone Traders of NamakMandi market at Pakistani Airports
Snippet: Purpose: This paper analyses the views and experiences of gemstone traders at the NamakMandi (NM) gemstone market. 
Methodology: The paper draws on the data from a stakeholder’s workshop held at Bacha Khan University Charsadda (Pakistan) and ten (10) semi-structured interviews primarily with traders, which were conducted as part of a larger research project for identifying factors inhibiting the beneficiation of gemstones in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan. 
Findings: The paper demonstrates that while the advent of the internet has ushered in quite a new era in the gemstone trade, particularly triggering higher interest among youth to initiate online gemstone businesses, but they are improvising and experimenting in an environment that is completely devoid of any official regulatory environment or support. In the face of the absence of relevant laws and regulations, the employees of the customs department at the airport resort to extortions and bribes both during the exportation and importation of gemstones in Pakistan. 
Implications: Unless an appropriate regulatory and supportive environment is created, online gemstone businesses may have a very sluggish growth, thus, taping its potential to create income-earning opportunities and revenue for the government.

Title: Zimbabwe's coloured gemstone endowments - A regional geological overview
Snippet: A gemstone is a mineral, rock, or other material that is prized for its beauty, durability, and rarity. Coloured gemstones are gemstones other than diamond (GIA, 1999); an alternative definition to the older subdivision that recognized precious (superior) versus semi-precious (inferior) gemstones (GIA, 1999;Lurie, 2000). Diamond, emerald, ruby, sapphire, and pearls were considered precious and the rest of the gemstones such as amethyst, tourmaline, aquamarine, citrine, and garnet were designated semi-precious (Lurie 2000). In the newer, preferred GIA (1999) definition, gemstones other than diamond include amber, ivory, and coral, which are organic materials (GIA, 1999;Lurie, 2000), thus gemstones need not necessarily be inorganic and crystalline. 

Although Zimbabwe has a significant gemstone endowment, the country is better known for its platinum group metals, chromite, gold, diamond, and coal resources (Bartholomew 1990). There is less awareness of the country's non-diamond (coloured) gemstone endowment. A notable exception is the global acclaim of the exquisite green Sandawana emeralds, discovered in 1956(Tyndale-Biscoe, 1968; Bartholomew, 1990), which firmly established the country as one of the emerald capitals of the world. Zimbabwean aquamarine and alexandrite have also earned global recognition, and are mentioned in international general gemmology textbooks such as Cipriani and Borelli (1986) and Read (2005). snippet.text:
Industry: The colored gemstone industry reveals three peculiarities. First, the stones vary largely in their value per carat, depending on the characteristics of the stone, such as scarcity, quality, origin, and customer attractiveness. Hence, assessing the characteristics of a stone is key for evaluating the value of a colored gemstone. Second, the value chain in the colored gemstone industry is highly complex and heterogeneous. There are many artisanal mines and only a few large-scale mines with heavy machinery on the mining stage. These are followed by traders that have either a regional, national, or international customer networks, refiners with diverse specializations in terms of cut and treatment, exporters, regional, national, and international wholesalers, jewelers, and retail brands [18]. Third, the transactions within the industry are based on mutual trust and reputation between transaction partners (e.g., miners and regional traders). A large volume of the trade is informal with limited transparency for external parties, causing substantial challenges for financing, insurance, and ethical standards. The previously described three peculiarities turned into a burden given the lack of transparency in the industry. First, for end-customers or upstream actors (e.g., retail brands), the actions of previous stages in the value chain are not transparent given the complexity and heterogeneity of the value chain as well as the informal transactions. Hence, buyers fear to finance unethical or ecological harmful actions in the downstream value chain. Second, end-customer as layperson having a hard time assessing the characteristics of a stone and its value. Consequently, end-customers are expecting more transparency on aspects such as origin, authenticity, and physical qualities. 

Blockchain application: Against this backdrop, Gübelin Gem Lab1 and Everledger2 introduced the Provenance Proof Blockchain3 for the colored gemstone industry. The blockchain solutions allow creating a digital twin for each colored gemstone and storing all relevant information (e.g., physical dimensions, color, cut) along the value chain. Each stage in the value chain has its own role and enables to upload of role-specific information.

Purpose: This paper analyses the views and experiences of gemstone traders at the NamakMandi (NM) gemstone market. 
Methodology: The paper draws on the data from a stakeholder’s workshop held at Bacha Khan University Charsadda (Pakistan) and ten (10) semi-structured interviews primarily with traders, which were conducted as part of a larger research project for identifying factors inhibiting the beneficiation of gemstones in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan. 
Findings: The paper demonstrates that while the advent of the internet has ushered in quite a new era in the gemstone trade, particularly triggering higher interest among youth to initiate online gemstone businesses, but they are improvising and experimenting in an environment that is completely devoid of any official regulatory environment or support. In the face of the absence of relevant laws and regulations, the employees of the customs department at the airport resort to extortions and bribes both during the exportation and importation of gemstones in Pakistan. 
Implications: Unless an appropriate regulatory and supportive environment is created, online gemstone businesses may have a very sluggish growth, thus, taping its potential to create income-earning opportunities and revenue for the government.

Title: Dynamic Analysis of Ruby Price Changes on Future Trends in the Jewelry Market Based on Genetic Algorithm Model
Snippet: Ruby is one of the important gemstones in jewelry, and its price changes have an important impact on the entire jewelry market. The supply and demand relationship of ruby is a key factor affecting its price. If supply decreases or demand increases, the price of rubies may increase. Conversely, if supply increases or demand decreases, ruby prices may fall. The stability of ruby prices is crucial to the development of the jewelry market. Large price fluctuations may lead to increased market uncertainty, affecting consumer purchasing decisions and industry stability. Changes in ruby prices may affect consumer demand for ruby jewelry. If prices rise, consumers may look for substitutes or reduce purchases, affecting market demand. On the contrary, lower prices may stimulate consumer interest in purchasing ruby jewelry. Movements in ruby prices may also be affected by external factors. 

Changes in ruby prices have an important impact on the jewelry market. Factors such as supply and demand, market stability, changes in consumer demand and external factors interact to determine the price trend in the ruby market. Participants in the jewelry industry should pay close attention to changes in ruby prices and make appropriate adjustments and decisions based on market conditions.

Title: Dynamic Analysis of Ruby Price Changes on Future Trends in the Jewelry Market Based on Genetic Algorithm Model
Snippet: : As a precious gemstone, ruby's price fluctuations have an important impact on the jewelry market. However, accurate analysis of ruby price trends and their impact on the future of the jewelry market has been difficult. This article aims to reveal the impact mechanism of ruby price changes on the future trend of the jewelry market through dynamic analysis based on a genetic algorithm model. To achieve this goal, we collected relevant data including supply and demand data, market stability indicators, changes in consumer demand and external factors, and applied genetic algorithm models for analysis. Through the analysis of data and the operation of the model, this article has obtained the trend prediction of ruby prices and the impact of price changes on the jewelry market. The contribution of this study is to provide a dynamic analysis method based on a genetic algorithm model, which can more accurately predict the trend of ruby prices, and provide an in-depth analysis of the factors affecting the price changes on the jewelry market. These research results provide important references for practitioners in the jewelry industry, allowing them to better understand market dynamics and make appropriate decisions. At the same time, this study also provides reference and inspiration for future research on dynamic analysis of trends in the jewelry market.

attempts.answer:
Summary
Synthetic diamonds are typically priced lower than natural diamonds for three main reasons: differences in production cost structures (lab growth vs. mining, cutting, and retail), market institutions and perceptions that depress the price of “synthetic” identity stones, and optical characteristics where slightly lower refractive indices and distinctive fluorescence/birefringence patterns can reduce perceived brilliance relative to well-graded naturals. These factors outweigh the optical advantage that natural diamonds have from a higher refractive index and help explain why synthetics command lower prices despite sometimes comparable or better physical properties on lab-controlled batches. <cite id="8378d59a-0">Diamond’s refractive index in the visible is about 2.4–2.7, enabling strong total internal reflection, while nanostructured or impurity-bearing CVD films can be 2.32–2.54</cite><cite id="8378d59a-3">Diamond’s refractive index of ~2.4 yields a small critical angle for total internal reflection, making sparkle highly dependent on n and cut</cite><cite id="824d6783-0">Identifying whether a diamond is natural or lab-grown is a key factor in market value for graders and appraisers</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Costs of lab-grown diamonds are typically 20–30% cheaper than mined ones</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">When color, size, shape, and purity are equal, lab-grown stones are still often priced lower due to customer stereotypes</cite>.

Optical basis: refractive index and brilliance
- Mechanistically, brilliance depends on how strongly light undergoes total internal reflection inside the stone, which depends on refractive index and cut. Higher refractive index lowers the critical angle, making TIR more efficient and enhancing brilliance under comparable lighting and cut quality. <cite id="8378d59a-3">Diamond’s refractive index of 2.4 gives a critical angle of 24.6°, much lower than glass (1.5 → 40.5°), so more light is reflected within the stone for a given facet geometry</cite>. 
- In practice, CVD synthetic diamonds grown today often have refractive indices slightly below 2.5 and can show distinct absorption features (e.g., 737 nm Si–V lines) and abnormal birefringence/interference colors, which can alter fluorescence patterns and perceived scintillation relative to natural Type IIa stones. <cite id="8378d59a-0">In the 1.24–5 eV range (visible) diamond n≈2.4–2.7; nanostructured CVD films show n≈2.32–2.54 depending on structure and impurities</cite><cite id="824d6783-4">CVD synthetics often show orange–red or mottled fluorescence under UV, with growth-layer patterns and phosphorescence behaviors distinct from naturals</cite><cite id="824d6783-2">Colorless/near-colorless CVDs exhibit abnormal birefringence and interference colors, and characteristic silicon-related photoluminescence peaks around 736.5–736.9 nm</cite><cite id="824d6783-3">CVDs display grainy, patchy birefringence patterns and higher-order interference colors than naturals at the same magnification</cite>. 
- Net effect: even though synthetics can match or surpass naturals on purity and clarity, their slightly lower average n and characteristic fluorescence/birefringence can reduce perceived brilliance in some color grades unless expertly cut and graded, leading buyers to discount value relative to comparably graded naturals. <cite id="8378d59a-3">Brilliance arises from TIR efficiency that increases with higher refractive index</cite><cite id="824d6783-1">CVDs commonly show 737 nm Si–V absorption, aiding identification but also altering optical response compared with naturals</cite><cite id="824d6783-0">Graders emphasize luminescence and specialized tools like DiamondView to detect identities that affect value</cite>. 

Certification, identity, and market psychology
- Professional certification stresses diamond “origin” as a primary attribute because it materially affects price. Instruments like De Beers’ DiamondView excite near the 225 nm absorption edge to reveal luminescence signatures that distinguish synthetic from natural, embedding identity into valuation. <cite id="824d6783-0">Appraisers and graders routinely test for luminescence under LW/SW UV; DiamondView uses <225 nm to authenticate and differentiate synthetics vs. naturals because origin is key to market value</cite>. 
- Retail narratives and grading emphasis amplify price gaps: even when physical/optical properties are comparable, synthetics tend to be devalued by 20–30% because customers and channels stereotype “lab” stones as lower value, and certification reports often highlight origin prominently. <cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Lab-grown diamond costs are 20–30% cheaper than mined, yet stakeholders attempt to preserve a marketing “dam” between the two flows</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">With equal color, size, shape, and purity, lab-grown stones are still typically priced lower due to customer stereotypes</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-1">Despite De Beers’ market share decline, average rough/polished prices rose and margins stayed high; industry behavior mimics monopoly pricing via collusion</cite>. 
- Color and clarity profiles also matter. CVDs can be grown to high color and clarity, but many commercial lots show silicon-related absorption and growth zoning; these features, along with fluorescence colors/kinetics, are used by graders to infer origin and adjust price downward when buyers expect naturals. <cite id="824d6783-2">Colorless/near-colorless CVDs show silicon-related PL peaks and lamellar growth with mottled fluorescence, differing from natural nitrogen-aggregated signatures</cite><cite id="824d6783-4">As CVD tech advances, fluorescence colors have converged toward naturals, but many still show distinctive patterns; early unannealed CVDs often appear red/orange under UV</cite>. 

Cost structures and market power
- Production costs diverge sharply: mining involves large capital and operating costs (ore extraction, sorting, cutting/faceting, distribution), while lab growth concentrates costs in capital equipment and gas/energy, with per-carat manufacturing costs that scale much more favorably for targeted, high-quality grades. <cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Lab-grown diamonds’ costs are 20–30% cheaper than mined; synthesis of 1 carat can take hours depending on process</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">Lab-growers targeting colorless, market-demanded stones realize more attractive prices than mined stones when parameters match, yet customers still stereotype lower values</cite>. 
- Industry structure has historically supported higher retail premiums over costs: despite De Beers’ decline from near-monopoly to a ~35% rough-value share, prices and margins have remained high, suggesting enduring oligopolistic coordination or signaling that suppresses price competition. <cite id="c1f2a63e-1">De Beers ≈35% of rough value; average rough/polished prices rose even as share declined, with high operating margins; behavior mimics De Beers’ monopoly via collusion</cite>. 
- Channel dynamics and consumer perception further widen spreads: retailers price by the 4Cs (carat, cut, color, clarity) and brand narratives, and certification reports that flag “lab-grown” can trigger lower premiums despite comparable optics; conversely, when synthetics improve quality (near-colorless, VS–SI clarity), prices compress but still reflect stigma and supply/demand shocks. <cite id="c1f2a63e-2">Natural diamond prices move via a chain of valued and taxed handling by dealers, cutters, and retailers; engagement ring demand fell in 2023, challenging “forever” narratives</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-4">Lab-grown capacity expansions drove prices down; lab-grown diamonds flooded markets, lowering both lab-grown and natural prices; De Beers’ 4Cs standardization shaped trade and pricing</cite>. 

Putting it together: why synthetics are cheaper even with “lower n”
- Mechanically, synthetics’ slightly lower refractive indices and distinctive fluorescence/birefringence can reduce brilliance or create mottling relative to comparably graded naturals, so buyers demand lower prices for equal grades unless expertly cut and presented. <cite id="8378d59a-3">Higher n increases TIR efficiency and brilliance for a given cut</cite><cite id="824d6783-2">CVDs show abnormal birefringence/interference and silicon-related luminescence distinct from naturals</cite><cite id="824d6783-0">Luminescence testing under UV/DiamondView is standard because origin materially affects value</cite>. 
- Institutionally, certification and retail standards embed “synthetic” identity into pricing, and buyer stereotypes depress premiums even when properties are comparable; this effect is magnified by the historical pricing power of the mined-diamond oligopoly. <cite id="c1f2a63e-3">With identical parameters, lab-grown stones are still typically priced lower due to customer stereotypes</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-1">Average diamond prices and margins have remained high despite De Beers’ decline, with collusion-like behavior</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Stakeholders have sought to build a marketing dam between mined and lab-grown flows</cite>. 
- Economically, lab-grown production focuses capital and energy into targeted, high-quality output and achieves lower per-carat costs than mining’s dispersed, quality-variable rough; however, retail channels still apply lower premiums to “lab-grown” identities and to color grades that show diagnostic fluorescence/birefringence patterns. <cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Lab-grown diamond costs are 20–30% cheaper than mined</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">Lab-growers selling colorless, market-demanded stones can achieve better average prices than mined but face stereotype-driven discounts</cite><cite id="824d6783-4">Even as CVD fluorescence approaches natural-like colors, graders detect distinctive patterns that influence value</cite>. 

Caveats and exceptions
- Quality tiers flip the script: top colorless/near-colorless synthetics grown without detectable silicon absorption or with superior cut can rival or exceed naturals on brilliance and purity, and their lower manufacturing costs still yield attractive price premiums; market acceptance and retailer assortments are converging, narrowing spreads. <cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Synthesis can produce 1 carat in hours; chemically pure, technologically controlled lab-grown diamonds enable many industrial and optical uses</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">When parameters are equal, lab-grown stones are often priced lower due to stereotypes, but high-quality focused producers can achieve better average prices</cite>. 
- Optical comparisons are nuanced: while refractive index differences exist, brilliance also depends on cut, polishing, and fluorescence/absorption profiles; some synthetics exhibit improved color uniformity and fluorescence behaviors that can rival or surpass naturals. <cite id="824d6783-4">CVD fluorescence colors have converged toward naturals in recent years, with some showing near-natural appearance under DiamondView</cite><cite id="8378d59a-0">Refractive index differences between diamond and nanostructured CVD films reflect material/structural variation, not a universal rule</cite>. 

Bottom line
Synthetic diamonds’ lower prices versus naturals reflect a balance of physics, certification, and economics: slightly lower refractive indices and distinctive optical signatures can reduce perceived brilliance relative to well-graded naturals, certification and retail narratives embed a “synthetic” discount, and lab-grown manufacturing concentrates costs in ways that still undercut mining/cutting/retail overlays even as channel stigma persists. <cite id="8378d59a-3">Diamond’s high refractive index supports efficient TIR and sparkle, so lower n in many synthetics can reduce brilliance unless cut and grade compensate</cite><cite id="824d6783-0">Origin testing via UV luminescence and DiamondView is central to valuation because it changes market value</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Lab-grown costs are typically 20–30% lower than mined, providing a structural price edge</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">Customer stereotypes depress prices even when parameters match, reinforcing lower premiums for lab-grown stones</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-1">Industry structure and collusion-like behavior have sustained high prices and margins, limiting competitive pressure on premiums</cite>. As lab-grown quality improves and acceptance grows, price gaps narrow by grade, but the combination of optics, certification, and cost structures explains why synthetics are generally cheaper today. <cite id="c1f2a63e-2">Market dynamics, including demand shocks and capacity releases, have pressured both lab-grown and natural diamond prices, while certification standards (4Cs) continue to shape valuation</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-4">Despite recent downturns, consumer segments in China and elsewhere sustain diamond jewelry demand, yet lab-grown capacity expansions have already lowered prices</cite>.

Title: Spectral Characteristics of Nitrogen-Doped CVD Synthetic Diamonds and the Origin of Surface Blue Fluorescence
Snippet: In the PL spectra, the as-grown samples generally have luminescence peaks caused by nitrogen-related defects, such as the 637 nm peak, which is attributed to the negatively charged N-vacancy optical defects NV − [31] and the 575 nm peak of the NV 0 center [32,33], but lack the H3 (NVN 0 ) center (with ZPL at 503.2 nm) caused by a defect with two nitrogen atoms adjacent to a single vacancy (Figure 9) [34,35]. The broad UV-Vis absorption band at ~270 nm and absorption step at 360 nm are likely caused by isolated ppm-level nitrogen [5,30]. Based on this absorption peak, it is implied that the diamond is CVD synthetic, HPHT synthetic (Ib-type), or HPHT-treated natural diamond (type-II) [36]. The luminescence under DiamondView varies with the type of defects in the diamond. Most unprocessed CVD synthetic diamonds have usually orange-red/-yellow fluorescence due to the dominance of NV defects [1,37]. Meanwhile, there is no discernible 1344 cm −1 absorption peak in the IR spectra. This indicates that the samples are type IIa with trace nitrogen, consistent with the orange-red fluorescence under DiamondView. 

Pure CVD synthetic diamonds are nitrogen-free type IIa. The growth rate of CVD diamonds can be significantly increased by doping trace amounts of nitrogen [38]. Type IIa CVD synthetic diamonds (no discernible absorption at 1344 cm −1 ) can be grown even when doped with nitrogen [11]. Nitrogen-doped CVD synthetic diamonds are usually brown and less appealing than other colors due to the introduction of nitrogen vacancies and hydrogen complexes [11]. Snippet: Diamond is transparent over a large range of wavelengths [from the ultraviolet (UV) to the far-IR]. Moreover, its large bandgap (5.47 eV) prevents thermally generated conduction at elevated temperatures. Therefore diamond remains transparent even at very high temperatures and radiation intensities. Diamond is thus an ideal material for optical applications, and can be used as X-ray and UV-transparent windows, and X-ray dosimeters. 

The sparkling of a diamond is caused by an optical phenomenon called Total Internal Reflection (TIR). The light undergoes many internal reflections inside the diamond before it exits. When light crosses a boundary from a medium with a higher to one with a lower refractive index, the light will be partially refracted at the boundary surface, and partially reflected. At a certain critical angle, light is refracted such that it travels along the boundary. When the incidence angle is greater than the critical angle, all of the light will be reflected. This is called TIR. Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence (TIRF) spectroscopy makes use of this principle to study events at or close to the interface of two different media, for instance the analysis of cells on a coverslip in biological applications. The higher the refractive index of the material at the side of the incoming light beam with respect to the refractive index of the material at the other side of the boundary, the lower the critical angle at which TIR is obtained, and facilitating TIRF applications. The refractive index of diamond is 2.4, leading to a critical angle of 24.6°. This is much lower than for glass, having a refractive index of 1.5, and hence a critical angle of 40.5° [25].
</snippet>

Snippet: Gemological characteristics of colorless and near-colorless CVD synthetic diamonds with different color grades produced by Zhengshi Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China, were studied and compared with the same color grade of natural diamonds. All the CVD samples belong to type IIa and have little nitrogen, silicon, and hydrogen impurities, while natural diamonds are of type Ia. Colorless or near-colorless CVD diamonds have obvious abnormal birefringence and interference. A high color grade of CVD diamond has less abnormal birefringence and low-order interference, while a low color grade of CVD diamond has obvious abnormal birefringence and high-order interference color. UV-Vis spectra results show CVD diamonds have a small amount of isolated nitrogen, while natural diamonds have aggregated nitrogen and some low color grade samples have a small amount of hydrogen. PL spectra indicate that CVD diamonds have the characteristic absorption peaks of silicon, and natural diamonds have the absorption peaks of aggregated nitrogen. The colorless CVD diamonds show blue, orange red, purple red, and blue with mottled fluorescence, while natural diamonds show mainly blue fluorescence. CVD samples show lamellar growth and mottled luminescence pattern, and natural diamonds show irregular ring-like growth structure. So, multiple methods are needed to distinguish CVD synthetic diamonds from natural diamonds.

Snippet: De Beers now produces approximately 35 percent of the world's rough diamonds by value (around 25 percent by volume), with Alrosa (Russia's production company) controlling approximately 30 percent (27 percent by volume), and three other competitors each producing between 2 and 10 percent (Bain & Co., Inc. 2015, p. 10). One might expect that because diamond production is no longer dominated by a monopolist and now involves several smaller players, diamond prices would be less stable and would sway with the vicissitudes of speculation and demand. Since the economic downturn of 2009, however, diamond prices have remained stable compared with other precious commodities (see Figure 2).

Theory would also predict that a less concentrated market would yield lower wholesale prices and lower monopoly rents, but here too the opposite has occurred. As De Beers' market share declined since the turn of the millennia, average prices per carat, for both rough and polished diamonds, have increased (see Figure 3), and average operating margins among leading diamond producers have also remained high, even after the global downturn in 2009 (see Figure 4).

How has the diamond industry retained (and in some cases, amplified) monopolistic features even after the decline of De Beers' notorious monopoly? 6 Longtime industry watchdog Chaim Even-Zohar suggests that the diamond oligopoly is mimicking many of the pricing behaviors of the De Beers monopoly, in part due to collusion (Even-Zohar 2015). Summary
Synthetic diamonds are typically priced lower than natural diamonds for three main reasons: differences in production cost structures (lab growth vs. mining, cutting, and retail), market institutions and perceptions that depress the price of “synthetic” identity stones, and optical characteristics where slightly lower refractive indices and distinctive fluorescence/birefringence patterns can reduce perceived brilliance relative to well-graded naturals. These factors outweigh the optical advantage that natural diamonds have from a higher refractive index and help explain why synthetics command lower prices despite sometimes comparable or better physical properties on lab-controlled batches. <cite id="8378d59a-0">Diamond’s refractive index in the visible is about 2.4–2.7, enabling strong total internal reflection, while nanostructured or impurity-bearing CVD films can be 2.32–2.54</cite><cite id="8378d59a-3">Diamond’s refractive index of ~2.4 yields a small critical angle for total internal reflection, making sparkle highly dependent on n and cut</cite><cite id="824d6783-0">Identifying whether a diamond is natural or lab-grown is a key factor in market value for graders and appraisers</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Costs of lab-grown diamonds are typically 20–30% cheaper than mined ones</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">When color, size, shape, and purity are equal, lab-grown stones are still often priced lower due to customer stereotypes</cite>.

Optical basis: refractive index and brilliance
- Mechanistically, brilliance depends on how strongly light undergoes total internal reflection inside the stone, which depends on refractive index and cut. Higher refractive index lowers the critical angle, making TIR more efficient and enhancing brilliance under comparable lighting and cut quality. <cite id="8378d59a-3">Diamond’s refractive index of 2.4 gives a critical angle of 24.6°, much lower than glass (1.5 → 40.5°), so more light is reflected within the stone for a given facet geometry</cite>. 
- In practice, CVD synthetic diamonds grown today often have refractive indices slightly below 2.5 and can show distinct absorption features (e.g., 737 nm Si–V lines) and abnormal birefringence/interference colors, which can alter fluorescence patterns and perceived scintillation relative to natural Type IIa stones. <cite id="8378d59a-0">In the 1.24–5 eV range (visible) diamond n≈2.4–2.7; nanostructured CVD films show n≈2.32–2.54 depending on structure and impurities</cite><cite id="824d6783-4">CVD synthetics often show orange–red or mottled fluorescence under UV, with growth-layer patterns and phosphorescence behaviors distinct from naturals</cite><cite id="824d6783-2">Colorless/near-colorless CVDs exhibit abnormal birefringence and interference colors, and characteristic silicon-related photoluminescence peaks around 736.5–736.9 nm</cite><cite id="824d6783-3">CVDs display grainy, patchy birefringence patterns and higher-order interference colors than naturals at the same magnification</cite>. 
- Net effect: even though synthetics can match or surpass naturals on purity and clarity, their slightly lower average n and characteristic fluorescence/birefringence can reduce perceived brilliance in some color grades unless expertly cut and graded, leading buyers to discount value relative to comparably graded naturals. <cite id="8378d59a-3">Brilliance arises from TIR efficiency that increases with higher refractive index</cite><cite id="824d6783-1">CVDs commonly show 737 nm Si–V absorption, aiding identification but also altering optical response compared with naturals</cite><cite id="824d6783-0">Graders emphasize luminescence and specialized tools like DiamondView to detect identities that affect value</cite>. 

Certification, identity, and market psychology
- Professional certification stresses diamond “origin” as a primary attribute because it materially affects price. Instruments like De Beers’ DiamondView excite near the 225 nm absorption edge to reveal luminescence signatures that distinguish synthetic from natural, embedding identity into valuation. <cite id="824d6783-0">Appraisers and graders routinely test for luminescence under LW/SW UV; DiamondView uses <225 nm to authenticate and differentiate synthetics vs. naturals because origin is key to market value</cite>. 
- Retail narratives and grading emphasis amplify price gaps: even when physical/optical properties are comparable, synthetics tend to be devalued by 20–30% because customers and channels stereotype “lab” stones as lower value, and certification reports often highlight origin prominently. <cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Lab-grown diamond costs are 20–30% cheaper than mined, yet stakeholders attempt to preserve a marketing “dam” between the two flows</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">With equal color, size, shape, and purity, lab-grown stones are still typically priced lower due to customer stereotypes</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-1">Despite De Beers’ market share decline, average rough/polished prices rose and margins stayed high; industry behavior mimics monopoly pricing via collusion</cite>. 
- Color and clarity profiles also matter. CVDs can be grown to high color and clarity, but many commercial lots show silicon-related absorption and growth zoning; these features, along with fluorescence colors/kinetics, are used by graders to infer origin and adjust price downward when buyers expect naturals. <cite id="824d6783-2">Colorless/near-colorless CVDs show silicon-related PL peaks and lamellar growth with mottled fluorescence, differing from natural nitrogen-aggregated signatures</cite><cite id="824d6783-4">As CVD tech advances, fluorescence colors have converged toward naturals, but many still show distinctive patterns; early unannealed CVDs often appear red/orange under UV</cite>. 

Cost structures and market power
- Production costs diverge sharply: mining involves large capital and operating costs (ore extraction, sorting, cutting/faceting, distribution), while lab growth concentrates costs in capital equipment and gas/energy, with per-carat manufacturing costs that scale much more favorably for targeted, high-quality grades. <cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Lab-grown diamonds’ costs are 20–30% cheaper than mined; synthesis of 1 carat can take hours depending on process</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">Lab-growers targeting colorless, market-demanded stones realize more attractive prices than mined stones when parameters match, yet customers still stereotype lower values</cite>. 
- Industry structure has historically supported higher retail premiums over costs: despite De Beers’ decline from near-monopoly to a ~35% rough-value share, prices and margins have remained high, suggesting enduring oligopolistic coordination or signaling that suppresses price competition. <cite id="c1f2a63e-1">De Beers ≈35% of rough value; average rough/polished prices rose even as share declined, with high operating margins; behavior mimics De Beers’ monopoly via collusion</cite>. 
- Channel dynamics and consumer perception further widen spreads: retailers price by the 4Cs (carat, cut, color, clarity) and brand narratives, and certification reports that flag “lab-grown” can trigger lower premiums despite comparable optics; conversely, when synthetics improve quality (near-colorless, VS–SI clarity), prices compress but still reflect stigma and supply/demand shocks. <cite id="c1f2a63e-2">Natural diamond prices move via a chain of valued and taxed handling by dealers, cutters, and retailers; engagement ring demand fell in 2023, challenging “forever” narratives</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-4">Lab-grown capacity expansions drove prices down; lab-grown diamonds flooded markets, lowering both lab-grown and natural prices; De Beers’ 4Cs standardization shaped trade and pricing</cite>. 

Putting it together: why synthetics are cheaper even with “lower n”
- Mechanically, synthetics’ slightly lower refractive indices and distinctive fluorescence/birefringence can reduce brilliance or create mottling relative to comparably graded naturals, so buyers demand lower prices for equal grades unless expertly cut and presented. <cite id="8378d59a-3">Higher n increases TIR efficiency and brilliance for a given cut</cite><cite id="824d6783-2">CVDs show abnormal birefringence/interference and silicon-related luminescence distinct from naturals</cite><cite id="824d6783-0">Luminescence testing under UV/DiamondView is standard because origin materially affects value</cite>. 
- Institutionally, certification and retail standards embed “synthetic” identity into pricing, and buyer stereotypes depress premiums even when properties are comparable; this effect is magnified by the historical pricing power of the mined-diamond oligopoly. <cite id="c1f2a63e-3">With identical parameters, lab-grown stones are still typically priced lower due to customer stereotypes</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-1">Average diamond prices and margins have remained high despite De Beers’ decline, with collusion-like behavior</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Stakeholders have sought to build a marketing dam between mined and lab-grown flows</cite>. 
- Economically, lab-grown production focuses capital and energy into targeted, high-quality output and achieves lower per-carat costs than mining’s dispersed, quality-variable rough; however, retail channels still apply lower premiums to “lab-grown” identities and to color grades that show diagnostic fluorescence/birefringence patterns. <cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Lab-grown diamond costs are 20–30% cheaper than mined</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">Lab-growers selling colorless, market-demanded stones can achieve better average prices than mined but face stereotype-driven discounts</cite><cite id="824d6783-4">Even as CVD fluorescence approaches natural-like colors, graders detect distinctive patterns that influence value</cite>. 

Caveats and exceptions
- Quality tiers flip the script: top colorless/near-colorless synthetics grown without detectable silicon absorption or with superior cut can rival or exceed naturals on brilliance and purity, and their lower manufacturing costs still yield attractive price premiums; market acceptance and retailer assortments are converging, narrowing spreads. <cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Synthesis can produce 1 carat in hours; chemically pure, technologically controlled lab-grown diamonds enable many industrial and optical uses</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">When parameters are equal, lab-grown stones are often priced lower due to stereotypes, but high-quality focused producers can achieve better average prices</cite>. 
- Optical comparisons are nuanced: while refractive index differences exist, brilliance also depends on cut, polishing, and fluorescence/absorption profiles; some synthetics exhibit improved color uniformity and fluorescence behaviors that can rival or surpass naturals. <cite id="824d6783-4">CVD fluorescence colors have converged toward naturals in recent years, with some showing near-natural appearance under DiamondView</cite><cite id="8378d59a-0">Refractive index differences between diamond and nanostructured CVD films reflect material/structural variation, not a universal rule</cite>. 

Bottom line
Synthetic diamonds’ lower prices versus naturals reflect a balance of physics, certification, and economics: slightly lower refractive indices and distinctive optical signatures can reduce perceived brilliance relative to well-graded naturals, certification and retail narratives embed a “synthetic” discount, and lab-grown manufacturing concentrates costs in ways that still undercut mining/cutting/retail overlays even as channel stigma persists. <cite id="8378d59a-3">Diamond’s high refractive index supports efficient TIR and sparkle, so lower n in many synthetics can reduce brilliance unless cut and grade compensate</cite><cite id="824d6783-0">Origin testing via UV luminescence and DiamondView is central to valuation because it changes market value</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-0">Lab-grown costs are typically 20–30% lower than mined, providing a structural price edge</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-3">Customer stereotypes depress prices even when parameters match, reinforcing lower premiums for lab-grown stones</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-1">Industry structure and collusion-like behavior have sustained high prices and margins, limiting competitive pressure on premiums</cite>. As lab-grown quality improves and acceptance grows, price gaps narrow by grade, but the combination of optics, certification, and cost structures explains why synthetics are generally cheaper today. <cite id="c1f2a63e-2">Market dynamics, including demand shocks and capacity releases, have pressured both lab-grown and natural diamond prices, while certification standards (4Cs) continue to shape valuation</cite><cite id="c1f2a63e-4">Despite recent downturns, consumer segments in China and elsewhere sustain diamond jewelry demand, yet lab-grown capacity expansions have already lowered prices</cite>. </answer>
